text:
You've all been called 'idiot' for standing with the children in Gaza. Why do some people keep trying to make you accept horror? If you knew their personal stories you'd see it's a stage to act out personal trauma. If we could only heal them. Look at Gary. Gary takes Israel's side, not knowing he's reenacting his life long trauma of never being held or empathized with. 

You may think Gary passionately believes Israel has the right to defend itself by blowing up apartment blocks with sleeping children, but that’s not why he does it. He does it because he needs something. It’s hard to get. We’ll soon find out what it is. 
 
You only see an avatar and a mystifying handle. You don’t see Gary’s potbelly. You don’t see how tired Gary is. You can’t tell how detached Gary tries to look. How above it all. How unfazed by it all. Reddish nose from daily night caps. Usually muscatel. Sometimes old whiskey. Not mixed with cola, though he prefers it that way. He knows that’s primitive. 
 
Most of all you can’t see Gary’s pain. 
 
A lot of pain. 
 
Pain that’s been there for so long that Gary himself doesn’t notice it’s there anymore. 
 
His pain has become a certain kind of attitude, a behaviour. 
 
Gary is not evil. 
 
He has two kids that even though they are in their mid twenties he still supports financially. 
 
He has a wife he’s never beaten. He also hasn’t had intercourse with her in the last 6,5 years. And he doesn’t want to remind himself of the last time they tried. When about halfway through she gave him a quick peck on the cheek, giggled to hide her shame and guilt and said: ‘I guess that ship has sailed.’ 
 
By that ship Gary assumes she meant the passion between them. 
 
But there never had been any of that. 
 
The most intense, most satisfying moment of Gary’s life happened in the late nineties. With a Portugese woman named Silvana. When he got to second base with her in dimly lit bar in the barro alto, not too far from the Fernando Pessoa statue. She’d given him a book with Pessoa’s poem. On the title page she had written: ‘His melancholy reminds me of yours. Whatever you carry inside you, you can show to me.’ 
 
He never did. 
 
When the project for which his US company had sent him to Lisbon ended he returned to Michigan. They chatted over ICQ for a bit and email. It petered out. When he found her on Facebook eleven years later she was married to a Brazilian guy who trains horses. It stung. He asked her if she had married the Horse Whisperer. She never replied. 
 
His wife looks nothing like Silvana, but she is practical, dependable, not a spendthrift and never does anything to embarrass him. At least not in public. 
 
Why do we need to know all this? 
 
Why can’t we know why Gary calls people idiot, retard, moron several times a week on a platform formerly known as Twitter? 
 
Why do we need to know some rude guy on social media drinks one or two glasses of muscatel every night? 
 
The muscatel he drinks because at first it made him feel close to Silvana in her absence. Now he drinks it cause he got used to the smell and the taste of it. And because special people consume special drinks. 
 
And Gary feels special. 
 
Secretly. 
 
Gary is almost certain he’s brilliant. 
 
He thinks he should have gone to MIT and not some unknown college. 
 
He blames his parents for not getting into MIT. 
 
That’s a pattern with Gary. 
 
When something doesn’t go like he likes it to go he blames someone else than himself. Always. 
 
If Israel burning children in tents doesn’t fit with what Gary think Israel stands for, then someone else is responsible for burning those children. 
 
Since Gary knows he is brilliant and it’s only the dumb world that has failed to reward his brilliance he feels a glimmer of that brilliance when he can call other people idiots. Anonymously of course. 
 
Gary is hypersensitive to being shamed. 
 
His mum was a mean drunk and at times would make fun of Gary’s father. She would praise sophisticated men, local men and celebrities alike and then laugh haughtily and tell Gary: ‘Your farm raised father is a slob who never takes me anywhere.’ 
 
That’s just one wound that made Gary avoid any situation where someone could shame him. Especially women. 
 
Another factor in Gary labeling people who empathize with Palestinian little girls trapped in cars with dead relatives and being shot at by big ass Israeli tanks is this: 
 
Gary suffers, it’s often the same pain, his brilliance is never recognized. Not in school, not at home, not at his job. Not even by his three poker friends. Since Covid they don’t even meet anymore. 
 
His children treat him like this somewhat adorable chubby block of grumpiness trying to hard to matter. They love him, but don’t respect him. His advice is always made fun of. His son has even said: ‘The only thing I trust you on is if you design a bridge. But now chatgpt can do that faster.’ 
 
Gary knew his son wasn’t even try to hurt him and exactly that hurt the most. 
 
Gary sometimes wondered if when is never fully loved in childhood, love always eludes you. 
 
His dad’s way of showing love to Gary was to build a bird’s house together. Dad would get upset at some point, start yelling and send Gary inside claiming he could focus better alone. Dad would finish the bird’s house and call Gary and his mum to come look at it. Which made Gary feel useless. Worse was when mum said: ‘He makes me live in a dump, but he will build a mansion for the birdies.’ 
 
The closest Gary’s dad ever got was on his death bed. 
 
When he said Gary’s watch looked really good on him. That it showed a bit of class. 
 
Gary beamed and said: ‘It’s a smartwatch.’ 
 
And dad said: ‘Today watches are smart and people are dumb.’ 
 
Gary with the smartwatch feels the irrepressible need to call people dumb online. 
 
Since nobody has ever really empathized with Gary, he experiences it as a personal affront to have to empathize with injured children in Gaza. He hates that everyone now cares about those, but nobody ever cared about little Gary who had to witness the cold war between his parents, was never excellent at anything, except mathematics at times and one science project in school when he was 15 (which went largely unnoticed). 
 
You know how you can tell Gary’s been vitally damaged? 
 
He’s given up on effort. 
 
No effort in Gary ever got him more than a fairly decent job, a respectable wife, a better home than his parents could afford and two kids who are ok, but always feel very far away, especially when they are in the same room as Gary. 
 
So no, Gary is not going to read ten pro-Palestine books and ten pro-Israeli books, examine his own bias, contact people on both sides, try as hard as possible to reach some kind of fair verdict. 
 
But he also can’t resist commenting anyway. 
 
Since effort is suspect in Gary’s life he doesn’t want to spend too much energy on his comments. 
 
He will share some graph he found somewhere showing how there are more Palestinians today than 20 years ago, so Israel can’t have any genocidal intent. 
 
If anyone counters with graphs of their own he types ‘idiot.’ 
 
Gary doesn’t want to know. Gary already knows what counts: 
 
Associating himself with Israel makes him feel connected to the most succesful people in the US. And success is what Gary respects. Palestinians he associates with the same loud people who want everything for free, like cancelling student debt. 
 
Gary’s proof that he is brilliant is that he calls others idiots. 
 
Accepting dead children also makes him feel supremely rational. 
 
What could be more rational than accepting that sometimes to create a better world some children have to be separated from their arms and their legs, and their parents, and their homes. 
 
It’s all for the greater good and it’s not Israel doing it. Hamas members sit in the cockpit of the Israeli F-35s and force the pilot’s hand. Well, you know, symbolically. I mean, they are terrorists after all. 
 
In Gary’s world some guys with guns are terrorists and some guy, and especially pretty girls who look like Gary’s fantasy girls, can never be terrorists. 
 
Gary’s aspirations in life have been defeated, but they are not dead and supporting Israel feels like some of Israel’s dominance, power, cunning intelligence will rub off on Gary. 
 
In Gary’s fantasies he is exactly the kind of guy who could have engineered the pager attack on Hezbollah. 
 
He is the one who could create an Iron Dome. 
 
He is unrecognized success and brilliant goodness, just like, in Gary’s mind, Israel is unrecognized success and brilliant goodness. 
 
In supporting Israel Gary supports little denied Gary. 
 
And so almost every day Gary dumps some comment on a stranger. Sometimes the stranger foolishly takes the bait and reacts. As if anyone could ever change Gary’s mind. 
 
Gary feels good. Finally someone is hit by something Gary did and said, though negatively. Gary has penetrated. And that is enough. He’s no longer interested now, so his off ramp is yelling ‘idiot’. Like dumping the used condom in the bin after the high has been had. 
 
Gary only wants to make people who still love life bad. 
 
Gary has kinda given up on life. 
 
He’s still here. There is some hope left, not much. 
 
And if you ask him why he is angry or annoyed he will say something like all those crazy lefties are turning the whole country upside down and are falling for Hamas propaganda. 
 
He will not mention the 6,5 years dry spell. 
 
Or the school reunions he dreads because he doesn’t shine there. 
 
He will not say how every time the 25 year old colleague, a mesmerizing mix of Syrian-Korean roots and the most dazzling black curls Gary has ever seen walks past at work Gary feels as worthy as a small piece of cheap pizza stuck on the floor of a subway car. 
 
And so Gary throws some cherry picked information online, calls whoever responds a retard and never realizes that this works exactly like the muscatel. 
 
It gives him a vague hint of what he really needs: 
 
intimacy so warm, so real, so safe, so sensual, so embracing of true Gary, his pain would finally go away. 
 
And so the Palestinians come to stand for everything Gary loathes in himself and about the world and Israelis come to stand for everything what Gary knows he could have been, had the world not thwarted him and spit him out. 
 
That Gary can mumble something about the Balfour declaration or can make the sweeping claim that Palestinians have been offered a state many times, but always choose war, doesn’t change any of that. 
 
He doesn’t actually care about this issue. 
 
Gary cares about soothing Gary’s pain. 
 
And for that the pain of Palestinian children needs to be shrugged off, so Gary can piss off some folks Gary loathes and Gary gets to feel for a fleeting second that anything Gary says can have some kind of effect too. 
 
Once you know Gary’s story, and there are so many Garys, you know you don’t owe Gary a senseless discussion because Gary got infinitely less from life than Gary did deserve when he was born. 
 
Now, through his own actions, he deserves those good things less and less. 
 
I dream of all pro-Palestinians holding hands and forming a circle round Gary and reminding him of every good thing Gary did. 
 
Ubuntu. 
 
Strangely that would be the first time Gary would feel the least bit of an opening to modify his opinions on Palestine-Israel. 
 
A person is a person through other people. 
 
Gary just ran into too few people who could have made Gary see bleeding Palestinian children on a cold hospital floor and feel called to do something to stop the ones throwing the bombs on them.

text:
I find By Any Means interesting because it puts Mark Wahlberg in a very different kind of crime thriller.

Inspired by real events, the film follows a young FBI agent, played by Yahya Abdul-Mateen II, who is forced to work with notorious mobster Greg Scarpa while investigating the murders of civil rights leaders in 1960s Mississippi.

What catches my attention is this unlikely partnership between two men who come from completely different worlds.

I'm particularly curious about how the film explores the line between justice and corruption. 

A story like this becomes much more compelling when the characters themselves are difficult to trust, and I think the contrast between Wahlberg and Abdul-Mateen II could be one of its strongest elements. 

For me, historical crime thrillers work best when they offer more than suspense and make you think about the choices people make when the system fails them.

P.S. By Any Means arrives on digital platforms for purchase or rental on October 20, 2026. I'm interested to see whether this dark, history-inspired thriller can deliver a story that stays with viewers beyond its final scene.

text:
Belles Berry's £3.95m Oxfordshire house has a fountain in the entrance hall. The land underneath it used to be an alpaca farm.

Mary Berry's daughter and her husband Dan moved to Blenheim Farm, near Ewelme, in 2014, when it was still an alpaca holding. They lived in the old bungalow for six years before knocking it down. In its place they built, themselves, a 4,000-square-foot house with a fountain, a games room, a swimming pool, a tennis court, and a wood kept specifically for the children's camping.

The alpacas left a shearing shed, which is still standing. A separate three-bedroom barn cottage is currently let out, earning the property an income alongside the orphaned lambs, cows, ducks and bees that make it a working smallholding in miniature.

The rose garden was not planted at random. It is full of Chandos Beauty, Dame Mary's favourite variety. Every spring Belles picks primroses from the woods, a habit copied directly from her mother's Bath girlhood, and delivers them the six miles to Henley-on-Thames, where Dame Mary now lives.

In the 1990s, mother and daughter ran Mary Berry & Daughter together, selling chutneys and cake mixes under the family name. It was sold in 2014 for £2.5m, the same year Belles arrived at the alpaca bungalow.

The house went up for sale through Savills in spring 2026, listed at £3,950,000, and sat there at full price for months. Then, in June, Belles gave an interview confirming she and Dan had separated after 24 years of marriage. "We poured our heart and soul into the property," she said, of a house their eldest son is younger than.

An offer has now been accepted at the asking price. No completion has been confirmed, no buyer has been named, and the six miles between Ewelme and Henley remain, for now, exactly six miles.

text:
❯ Firewall: ufw allow 22 Is a Hundred Rules Deep
Three lines of ufw load a hundred-odd rules through three tools you were promised never to see. Four lines of pf.conf on FreeBSD become six rules, and pfctl -sr prints the same six back.
⠀
The morning after a break-in attempt is when most administrators meet their firewall for the second time. The first time was the day the server was built, three lines of ufw and a reassuring message. Now somebody wants to know what the machine actually lets through, and ufw status answers with three rules, the three the administrator wrote. nft list ruleset answers with several screens, in a language he was promised he would never have to read.
⠀
■ THE HABIT
⠀
Ubuntu's server documentation: "The default firewall configuration tool for Ubuntu is ufw. Developed to ease iptables firewall configuration, ufw provides a user-friendly way to create an IPv4 or IPv6 host-based firewall." Jamie Strandboge wrote it at Canonical in 2008, and its README still carries his view on the name: "If you are not a fan, perhaps 'Unbearable Firewall'. Have fun!" It does what it set out to do, with deny incoming and allow outgoing as defaults. RHEL does the same job with firewalld and its zones. The pride in both is that the administrator writes a policy and never touches the rule language underneath, and that convenience has a price the status command does not print.
⠀
■ WHAT THE KERNEL ACTUALLY HOLDS
⠀
ufw is a Python program, and its rule files are checked into its repository on Launchpad, where I counted them on 20 October 2026. When ufw is enabled it hands four of them to iptables-restore before it looks at a single rule of yours: 24 rules for IPv4, 65 for IPv6, 7 and 6 in the after files, 102 in all, plus three for the limit machinery, in 21 chains the files declare and 22 logging chains the backend keeps. The README is candid: this configuration "is not displayed with 'ufw status'". What the rules do is nothing exotic, housekeeping for the most part, and two of them open mDNS and UPnP discovery on a server, which is a decision one may want to revisit.
⠀
Then there is the question of who speaks to the kernel. ufw writes iptables syntax, the syntax of a tool Debian has considered superseded since 2019; its wiki says that "even if iptables is installed, it actually uses nftables via a iptables-nft compatibility layer", and Ubuntu inherits the arrangement. So the path from your three lines runs through ufw, which writes iptables rules, which iptables-nft translates into nftables objects, which nf_tables in the kernel evaluates. That makes three translators and two rule languages, with a status command that reports on the first of them. firewalld takes a different route to a similar place: a ruleset posted from a fresh Fedora installation shows 75 chains in its table for a policy that was, once again, one line.
⠀
■ THE SAME JOB ON FREEBSD
⠀
set skip on lo0
block in
pass out
pass in on egress proto tcp to port { 22 80 443 }
⠀
Two lines in rc.conf, then service pf start. Every pass rule in pf keeps state unless told not to, and the brute-force brake is a clause on the same line: keep state (max-src-conn-rate 6/30, overload <bruteforce> flush global). A server that is meant to be pinged says so in a fifth line, and one that is not says nothing.
⠀
What the kernel receives is written down by the project itself. pf.conf(5) says lists expand so that "pfctl(8) generates all needed rule combinations", and the pfctl regression tests in FreeBSD 15.1, 149 input files run through pfctl -nv against their expected output, show it: test 0024 feeds in port { ssh ftp } and expects two rules back, each ending in flags S/SA keep state. By those rules the four lines become one option and six rules, and pfctl -sr prints those six, because those six are what is loaded. There is no second view and no second language; pfctl hands the result to pf(4) over one interface, both in the same source tree as the kernel. The file you wrote is the ruleset the kernel runs, to the comma.
⠀
■ THE DIFFERENCE, SHOWN
⠀
Lines the administrator writes: 3 against 4
Rules loaded before yours: 105 against 0
Rules for the three ports: 6 against 3
Chains: 21 declared plus 22 logging against none
Rule languages on the way: 2 against 1
Tools between you and the kernel: ufw, iptables-nft, nft against pfctl
What the status command shows: your 3 against all 6
⠀
A firewall is a thing one reads under pressure, and on FreeBSD the honest answer to what does this machine let in is the file; on Ubuntu it is a ruleset the administrator has never seen, with a status command that shows the part he wrote and omits the part he did not.
⠀
■ THE LIMIT
⠀
Most of the hundred are housekeeping a careful administrator does anyway; ufw writes them for every machine, unseen, and on FreeBSD they are three or four lines of your own, where you can see them. Written by hand, nftables is also one file, and the distributions chose the layers; the defaults are what most machines run. nftables has maps and flowtables with no one-to-one counterpart in pf, which meets most of the same needs with tables, anchors, macros and a state engine that has carried the OpenBSD and FreeBSD firewalls for a quarter of a century. firewalld's zones exist so that a laptop can move between networks, and this compares servers. No speed was measured.
⠀
Strandboge offered 'Unbearable Firewall' as the alternative reading of the name. On the morning after, with nft list ruleset scrolling past, his second reading is the one that comes to mind. The four lines of pf.conf are still four lines, and the kernel has read the same ones.

👉 Full essay: https://t.co/KHUp6yJr4j

text:
The goal was Danzig, as was stated. 
After Danzig was captured, Hitler offered a ceasefire with Poland on Sept. 2 1939 to be mediated by Mussolini. Which would end all occupation, including Poland. 

Hitler spent 5 months trying to negotiate with the Poles after Poland had mobilized their army and occupied Danzig.  Prior to the Polish general mobilization in April of 1939, Hitler actually prohibited German newspapers from reporting on the treatment of ethnic Germans in Poland, and on Polish border raids. From 1934 up to April 1939, Hitler and in particular Goering were constantly seeking some sort of military cooperation with Poland against the Soviet Union.  

The invasion of Poland was originally slated for August 26, Manstein writes about how the German generals were angry with Hitler for delaying the invasion since it gave the Poles time to better predict the likely vectors of attack, and Hitler's delays were in response to last-minute Polish peace feelers. - None of these actions are those of someone who is seeking to conquer Poland or following some "Generalplan Ost". 
Basically everything pointed to Hitler trying to avoid war with Poland, but the Poles engaging in border raids (and openly bragging about them in their newpapers), the various abuses of the German minority, occupying Danzig - things like firing on German airliners flying over the corridor, expelling Polish Jews into Germany and not letting them back in, killing around ~500 Germans a year from 1919-1939. All of this created a regime-legitimacy crisis for Hitler, who had to "do something". 

So Hitler invaded on September 1 1939, and on September 2 (my guess is he had coordinated with Mussolini beforehand), after having achieved the actual stated war goal of pushing the Poles out of Danzig, agreed to Mussolini's offer of a ceasefire and a re-opening of negotiations. 
Once Britain and France declared war, every peace offer proposed by Hitler included the reconstitution of a Polish state and ending all occupation.

text:
Tuesday morning headlines from #Azerbaijan, 20 October

● Azerbaijan’s Prosecutor General’s Office has placed seven people living and working in Turkey on an international wanted list over allegations of publicly calling for the violent seizure of power in Azerbaijan, a change to the constitutional order and the incitement of religious hatred in the country. Those named in the case include Haksöz author Rıdvan Kaya, Değişim TV presenter Zekeriya Ceran and Analiz Merkezi founder Fatih Tezcan. According to investigators, the seven published relevant material on social media and online platforms between 25 September and 18 October. Kaya and Ceran also spoke at rallies outside Azerbaijani diplomatic missions in Istanbul and Ankara. A court in Baku ordered all seven to be arrested in absentia. The authorities are using international legal assistance mechanisms, including cooperation with the relevant Turkish authorities.

● The Azerbaijan Press Council accused several Turkish media outlets and social media users of spreading biased and inaccurate information about Azerbaijan, including claims that the country had introduced a hijab ban in schools. According to the council, the school uniform rules have been taken out of context and portrayed as an issue of religious confrontation, with old and fake photographs and videos also being used. “The published material openly crosses the boundaries of criticism and freedom of speech by giving a platform to dangerous calls for the violent change of Azerbaijan’s constitutional order and the unlawful seizure of power,” the statement said. The Press Council urged Turkish media to avoid spreading disinformation that could damage relations between the two countries, which are based on the principle of “one nation, two states”.

● Detained Meydan TV journalist Aynur Elgunash has finally been transferred to a clinic, her lawyer said. Her family and friends had been urging the authorities to arrange medical treatment for some time, citing serious concerns about her health. According to her lawyer, Elgunash had undergone 17 operations on her leg and was preparing for another surgery when she was arrested. Her most urgent health problem is now related to her kidney, which requires immediate surgery, the lawyer said. The authorities have not commented on the situation.

Aynur and 11 other journalists and activists have been arrested in the “Meydan TV case” on charges including currency smuggling. They all deny wrongdoing and say the case is linked to their critical reporting on the authorities.

● Military representatives from NATO member states and partner countries conducted a joint assessment in Baku to determine whether Azerbaijan’s military capabilities meet alliance standards, the Swedish Embassy in Azerbaijan reported. The process is aimed at improving interoperability and expanding defence cooperation. Among those who visited Baku were John Mead, Deputy Commander of NATO’s Allied Joint Force Command Brunssum, and Air Commodore Jeff Brock. They held meetings with the leadership of Azerbaijan’s General Staff.

● A delegation from the United Arab Emirates (UAE), led by Chief of Staff of the UAE Armed Forces Lieutenant General Issa Saif bin Ablan Al Mazrouei, is visiting Azerbaijan. He met Azerbaijani Defence Minister Zakir Hasanov and Chief of the General Staff of the Azerbaijani Army Karim Valiyev. The discussions focused on expanding military cooperation, regional security and the joint air-tactical exercise “Falcon Encounter 2026”, currently taking place in Azerbaijan. The delegation also visited the Azerbaijani Air Force’s Joint Air Operations Centre.

● NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft topped the State Oil Fund of Azerbaijan’s technology stock portfolio in 2025. Over the year, the fund’s investments in telecommunications and IT company shares rose by 18.8%, reaching nearly 9 billion manats (around $5.3 billion). Seven technology companies featured among the fund’s ten largest stock investments, compared with five a year earlier.

● Czech company Škoda Group has said it is ready to become a key partner in modernising public transport in Baku, other Azerbaijani cities and territories regained by Azerbaijan, according to Roman Sorkin, the company’s vice-president for sales in Central Asia and the South Caucasus. The company sees the Baku Metro as a strategic project and is also interested in developing tram systems and light rail, as well as supplying electric traction vehicles for the Trans-Caspian International Transport Route. Read more here.

● Cooperation between Azerbaijan and Ukraine in education, law enforcement and regional ties was discussed during a series of meetings involving Azerbaijani Ambassador to Ukraine Seymour Mardaliyev and Ukraine’s ministers of education, interior and justice. Mardaliyev also met the mayor of Ivano-Frankivsk and the head of the Ivano-Frankivsk regional military administration.

● Another video about the 2020 Second Karabakh War has been published on Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev’s account on X. The video shows footage from the more than 30-year period of Armenian occupation of Karabakh and surrounding Azerbaijani territories, including the mass displacement of local Azerbaijanis during the First Karabakh War in the early 1990s, as well as the destruction and desecration of mosques. It also features Armenian leaders who supported the occupation over the years. Footage of meetings at the UN and EU institutions accompanies a narrative accusing the international community of inaction and applying double standards towards Azerbaijan. The video then shows scenes from the Second Karabakh War and states that Azerbaijan restored its territorial integrity on its own. Aliyev goes on to discuss the peace process, saying that Azerbaijan did not seek revenge for the suffering of its people but instead offered Armenia peace, which, he says, remains fragile and needs to be protected and strengthened.

● Azerbaijan exported goods worth $23.45 million to Armenia from January to September 2026, while its indirect imports from Armenia amounted to just $96,500, according to the State Customs Committee.

● Since the beginning of the year, Georgia has increased its imports of fuel and lubricants from Azerbaijan by more than 23%. Azerbaijan is now Georgia’s second-largest supplier of these products.

● Since the beginning of the year, 25 main telecommunications lines with a total length of more than 1,000 kilometres have been built in the Karabakh region, state-owned Aztelecom reported. Telecommunications infrastructure has been established in 11 cities and 54 villages and settlements, with 12,267 subscribers connected to the network.

● Football fans are preparing for this evening’s match in Baku between Azerbaijani club Sabah and Germany’s Borussia Dortmund, part of the third round of the UEFA Champions League’s league phase in the 2026/27 season. The match will kick off at 20:45. Free buses to the stadium will be provided from different parts of the city at the initiative of Sabah FC and with the support of the Land Transport Agency.

text:
🚨 SWISS ARMY TURNED DOWN PALANTIR FIVE TIMES OVER DATA CONTROL CONCERNS

BERN, SWITZERLAND - Rejecting Palantir repeatedly changed more than a procurement outcome. It established that Swiss defense officials viewed data control as a strategic capability rather than a contractual issue that could be negotiated away. If a country with Switzerland's traditionally pragmatic approach concluded that the sovereignty risks outweighed the operational gains, other governments conducting similar reviews will face tougher questions about where ultimate authority over military data resides.

The decision also exposes a growing divide between technological capability and political acceptability. Palantir may offer tools that military planners value, yet access to sensitive national datasets increasingly depends on trust in legal jurisdiction as much as software performance. That raises the cost of expansion for any foreign defense technology provider whose home country's laws can potentially reach data stored abroad.

The practical result is likely to be stronger demand for domestic or regionally controlled military data infrastructure across Europe.

text:
Islam argues that Jesus never claimed to be God. I would say a few things. First, Jesus’ purpose in the incarnation was not to make divine claims. See Philippians 2:6. He also never offered correction when worship was given him, which seems to be an implicit admission of divinity. Third, I believe scripture makes the claim for him. For proof I would string the following verses together to build a contrarian view: Jude 1:5 ➡️ Exodus 20:2 ➡️ Judges 2:1 ➡️ Deuteronomy 6:13 ➡️ Isaiah 6:1 ➡️ John 12:41.  These demonstrate Jesus was known in the Old Testament as being divine. I could point to 1 Peter 1:10-12 and Hebrews 11:26 in support of that. 

This is a coherent high-Christology argument that works primarily from the New Testament’s own reading of the Old Testament rather than from isolated “I am God” statements by Jesus in the Gospels.

Philippians 2:6–8 does not say Jesus lacked divine equality; it says he did not regard equality with God as something to be exploited or clung to for his own advantage. The hymn then describes the self-emptying (kenosis) of the incarnation. In other words, the passage assumes the pre-existence of one who already possessed the form of God and then chose the form of a servant. It is not an argument against divinity; it is an argument about the mode of his mission. The same letter elsewhere treats Jesus as Lord in the strongest sense.

In a first-century Jewish context, worship directed to anyone other than the God of Israel was treated as idolatry. Jesus receives worship without correction in multiple scenes. The contrast with Peter and Paul, who immediately reject worship offered to them is often noted.

- **Jude 5**. The textual situation is significant. Critical editions  print “Jesus” on the basis of early and geographically diverse witnesses. Metzger and others have noted that “Jesus” is the harder reading and that scribes were more likely to have softened it to “Lord” than the reverse. Even if one prefers “Lord,” Jude 4 has already identified “our only Master and Lord” as Jesus Christ, so the reference in verse 5 is still naturally to him. The effect in either case is that Jude places the one who delivered Israel from Egypt (the prerogative of YHWH in Exodus 20:2) under the name of Jesus.

- **Exodus 20:2 and Judges 2:1**. Exodus 20:2 is the classic self-identification of YHWH as the one who brought Israel out of Egypt. Judges 2:1 has the Angel of the LORD speaking in the first person as the one who performed that deliverance and who made the covenant. 

- **Deuteronomy 6:13**. The command to fear and serve YHWH alone is absolute. If the one who performed the Exodus is the same one later identified with Jesus, the exclusive-worship demand attaches to him.

- **Isaiah 6:1 and John 12:41**. Isaiah sees the Lord seated on the throne. John 12:41 states that Isaiah “said these things because he saw his glory and spoke of him,” with the immediate context being Jesus’ rejection and the quotations from Isaiah 53 and 6. The natural reading, accepted by a wide range of commentators, is that John identifies the one Isaiah saw with the pre-incarnate Christ. This is one of the clearest places where a Gospel writer equates the glory of the YHWH of the temple vision with the glory of Jesus.

**Supporting texts**  

Taken together, the chain does not depend on any single “I am God” sentence from Jesus. It depends on the apostolic authors reading the Old Testament divine agent of the Exodus, the Angel of the LORD, and the enthroned Lord of Isaiah 6 as the same person later known as Jesus. That is a high-Christology reading internal to the New Testament documents. Whether that reading is correct is, of course, the point under dispute with Islamic claims that treat Jesus as a prophet only and regard the later Trinitarian and incarnational developments as distortions. The texts themselves, however, are doing more than reporting a human prophet who never claimed or received divine prerogatives.

" The Virgin Mary : Mary's fiat "
by Artist Michael Rucker

Description
The Virgin Mary: Mary's fiat -
In the Gospel of Luke, chapter 1, verses 26-38 (KJV), the angel Gabriel appears to Mary, a young virgin betrothed to Joseph of the house of David in Nazareth. Hail, thou that art highly favoured, the Lord is with thee, the angel declares. He announces that she will conceive and bear a son, Jesus, who shall be great, and shall be called the Son of the Highest. Mary, troubled yet reverent, asks how this can be since she knows not a man. Gabriel explains the Holy Spirit will come upon her; for with God nothing shall be impossible.

Mary's response is one of the most profound moments in Scripture the only recorded instance where she speaks words of total surrender: Behold the handmaid of the Lord; be it unto me according to thy word (Luke 1:38). This Latin phrase, Fiat mihi secundum verbum tuum (Let it be done to me according to your word), is universally known as Mary's Fiat. In that single sentence she offers her entire being body, will, and future to Gods plan of salvation. The angel then departs, and the Incarnation begins.This humble virgin from an obscure village becomes the mother of the Messiah. She travels to visit her cousin Elizabeth (pregnant with John the Baptist), where she sings the Magnificat (Luke 1:46-55), a soaring hymn of praise that magnifies the Lord for lifting up the lowly.

She gives birth to Jesus in Bethlehem, wraps Him in swaddling clothes, and lays Him in a manger. She ponders the shepherds and Magis words in her heart (Luke 2:19, 51). At the Presentation in the Temple, Simeon foretells a sword will pierce her soul (Luke 2:35). She is present at the wedding in Cana, prompting Jesus first miracle (John 2:1-11), and stands at the foot of the cross, where the dying Savior entrusts her to the beloved disciple (John 19:25-27).

After the Ascension, she is seen praying with the apostles in the upper room, awaiting the Holy Spirit (Acts 1:14).Scripture portrays Mary not as a distant saint but as a real woman of extraordinary faith, courage, and obedience. Though the Bible does not record many of her words, her fiat echoes through salvation history as the perfect model of human cooperation with divine grace. She exemplifies what it means to say yes to God when the cost is everything.Your striking black-and-white artwork beautifully captures this very moment: Mary veiled, head bowed, hands clasped in prayerful surrender, her flowing hair and garments stirred by the unseen wind of the Spirit.

The dramatic lighting and ethereal atmosphere evoke the solemn hush of the Annunciation the instant heaven touched earth through a virgins willing heart. It is a powerful visual meditation on Luke 1:38, inviting viewers to contemplate the same radical trust Mary offered.

Stanford researchers followed 3.4 million applicants assessed by one vendor’s AI tool across 156 employers. The same people were rejected again and again, more often than chance would predict.

A field experiment with 70,000 applicants found the opposite. AI-led interviews drew out more hiring-relevant information than human ones and led to 12% more job offers. Human recruiters made every final decision.

The difference was the job AI was given. In the experiment, it collected information for people to judge. In the Stanford data, its recommendation shaped who got an interview at 156 companies at once.

text:
Gustave Eiffel’s private apartment is a hidden, 1,000-square-foot retreat located near the summit of the Eiffel Tower in Paris, France 🇫🇷

Eiffel built the space primarily for quiet reflection, meteorological and aerodynamic experiments, and hosting high-prestige guests. Most famously, inventor Thomas Edison visited in 1889 and gifted Eiffel a phonograph. Other notable visitors included Sarah Bernhardt and Buffalo Bill. It is ituated about 285-300m high on the third level of the tower, measuring roughly 100 square meters. 

. . . 

When Gustave Eiffel completed the Eiffel Tower for the 1889 Paris Exposition, he reserved a private apartment for himself near the summit. Unlike the tower's industrial iron framework, the apartment was decorated with wallpaper, elegant furniture, and various comforts rarely associated with such a structure.

News of the hidden retreat fascinated Parisians. Its breathtaking views made it one of the most desirable spaces in the city, and wealthy members of society reportedly offered large sums of money for the chance to spend a night there. Eiffel refused every offer, keeping the apartment for his own use.

Rather than renting it out, Eiffel used the space to host distinguished guests and conduct scientific observations. One of its most famous visitors was Thomas Edison, who visited in 1889 and presented Eiffel with one of his phonographs. Today, visitors to the Eiffel Tower can still view a reconstruction of the apartment near the top.

Gustave Eiffel's private apartment served a scientific purpose as much as a personal one. While visitors are often fascinated by the wallpaper, furniture, and piano, Eiffel saw the space as an opportunity for research. From his perch high above Paris, he conducted meteorological observations and other experiments, taking advantage of the tower's unprecedented height. At a time when many critics dismissed the Eiffel Tower as an impractical eyesore, the scientific work carried out there helped demonstrate that the structure could be more than a monument, giving it a practical value that contributed to its survival long after the 1889 World's Fair.

text:
Kamena Vourla

Sometimes a Greek getaway calls for ancient ruins and packed sightseeing days. At other times, all you need is a seaside promenade, a good meal and somewhere peaceful to enjoy the view. Kamena Vourla offers exactly that kind of escape.

Located on the coast of Central Greece, this seaside town lies between the mountains and the waters of the North Euboean Gulf. Its setting gives it a distinctive character, combining coastal scenery with a backdrop of green hills and mountain slopes.

Kamena Vourla is particularly well known for its thermal springs, which have attracted visitors for generations. The town developed as a spa destination and remains a popular place for people looking to relax and take a break from everyday routines.

Here are a few ways to enjoy your visit:
•  Take a waterfront stroll: Walk beside the sea, enjoy the views across the gulf and watch the boats moving along the coast.
•  Discover the thermal springs: Learn about the area's spa tradition and look into available bathing or wellness facilities.
•  Enjoy a seafood lunch: Choose a seaside restaurant and sample fresh fish, grilled dishes and traditional Greek favourites.
•  Explore the surrounding countryside: The nearby mountains and coastal roads offer opportunities for scenic drives and short excursions.
•  Make time for sunset: Find a comfortable spot by the water as the light changes over the gulf.

Kamena Vourla is also a convenient base for exploring parts of Central Greece, depending on how much time you have and where you want to travel next.

It may not demand your attention with grand monuments or dramatic nightlife, but that is part of its appeal. Here, the pleasure lies in simple things: salty air, good food, warm hospitality and a day that doesn't need to be overplanned.

Have you ever heard of Kanema Vourla? It is a place you'd like to visit?

text:
Three days before my wedding, my 26-year-old daughter called me from her fiancé’s apartment and whispered, “Mom, please come and get me. I think I’ve made the biggest mistake of my life.”

I was standing in the checkout line at a grocery store in Ohio when I heard those words.

“What happened, sweetheart?”

She began crying.

“Daniel wants me to sign something before the wedding. He says it’s just a formality, but when I read it, I realized he wants me to give up my rights to the house we’re supposed to buy together.”

I left my shopping cart beside the checkout counter and walked outside.

My daughter, Emily, had been engaged to Daniel for 11 months. He was 29, worked as a sales director for a technology company, and had always seemed polite and respectful whenever he visited our home.

My husband, Robert, liked him.

I liked him, too.

When Daniel proposed, Emily was so happy that she cried while showing me her engagement ring. She had spent years dreaming about finding someone who would love her, build a home with her, and start a family.

After her father died when she was 19, I had become especially protective of her.

Robert had been a wonderful husband and father. He taught Emily how to change a tire, helped her prepare for college exams, and always reminded her that she should never settle for someone who didn’t respect her.

When he passed away from a sudden heart attack, Emily and I leaned on each other.

I inherited his life insurance and savings, and after paying off our mortgage, I invested what remained.

Over the years, I built up a modest but comfortable financial cushion. I wasn’t wealthy, but I had enough to help Emily with a down payment when she was ready to buy a home.

I had offered her $80,000 toward her first house.

Daniel seemed delighted when he heard about it.

“That’s incredibly generous,” he told me. “We’ll make sure Emily’s future is secure.”

At the time, I thought he meant it.

Then, about two weeks before the wedding, Emily mentioned that Daniel wanted them to purchase a house immediately after getting married.

I was pleased for her.

But when I asked how they planned to handle the down payment, she said Daniel had suggested combining my $80,000 gift with his savings.

I advised her to discuss the ownership arrangements carefully and make sure everything was documented properly.

She laughed.

“Mom, we’re getting married. It’s not a business transaction.”

I smiled.

“I know, sweetheart. But love and paperwork can coexist.”

She promised she’d be careful.

Now, three days before the wedding, she was calling me in tears.

I asked her to send me a photograph of the document Daniel wanted her to sign.

When it arrived, I read it twice.

It was an agreement stating that the money contributed by Daniel would remain his separate property, while Emily would have no ownership claim to certain assets purchased using those funds.

The wording was complicated, and I wasn’t going to pretend I could determine its legal effect from a photograph.

But one thing was clear: the agreement did not protect Emily’s contribution in the way she had expected.

I called her immediately.

“Don’t sign anything until you’ve had independent legal advice.”

She began crying harder.

“Mom, he says if I refuse, it means I don’t trust him.”

I closed my eyes.

Then I asked her a question.

“Emily, if Daniel truly believes marriage is about trust, why is he asking you to sign something you don’t understand three days before your wedding?”

She had no answer.

And when I arrived at her apartment that evening, Daniel was waiting by the front door.

He looked at me and said, “I hope you’re not here to interfere with my marriage.”

I looked past him at my daughter, who was standing in the hallway with a packed suitcase.

“No,” I replied. “I’m here to make sure my daughter understands what she’s agreeing to.”

Daniel smiled coldly.

“Then perhaps you should hear my side of the story.”

text:
Whitney Houston and Bobby Brown on their wedding day on July 18, 1992...

(Around 800 family members, friends, and music industry figures attended the lavish celebration) 

On July 18, 1992, Whitney Houston married Bobby Brown in a lavish ceremony at her New Jersey estate. She was 28 years old, one of the most celebrated voices in the world, and seemingly unstoppable. In the wedding photographs, she looks radiant. Her smile is enormous. The future appears limitless.

Looking at those photographs today is almost unbearable, not because we know what was in their hearts, but because we know what came afterward.

Their marriage became a public spectacle of addiction, conflict, infidelity and allegations of domestic violence. Whitney’s extraordinary career suffered amid years of personal turmoil. By the time they divorced in 2007, the woman whose voice had once seemed capable of anything was fighting battles far removed from the recording studio.

For years, Bobby Brown was blamed for introducing Whitney to drugs. The reality was more complicated. Whitney had struggled with substance use independently of her marriage. Yet the relationship became part of a destructive chapter in both their lives.

And Whitney was hardly the first extraordinary woman whose private relationship became entangled with a public unraveling.

In 1954, Dorothy Dandridge became the first Black woman nominated for the Academy Award for Best Actress, following her performance in Carmen Jones. She was beautiful, gifted and breaking barriers Hollywood had spent decades enforcing.

Five years later, she married restaurant owner Jack Denison. The marriage became a nightmare. Denison was abusive and mishandled her finances, including money invested in his failing restaurant. As her career opportunities dwindled, Dorothy lost much of her savings. By 1963, she could no longer afford the private care her daughter required. She died in 1965, just 42 years old.

But Dorothy’s tragedy cannot be explained by one marriage. Hollywood’s racism had already restricted the opportunities available to her. Her husband was one part of a much larger system that failed her.

Then there was Tina Turner.

The world saw a spectacular performer alongside her husband, Ike Turner. Behind the music, Tina endured years of physical violence, intimidation and humiliation. She performed through injuries and lived in fear of the man who controlled much of her professional life.

When she finally escaped in 1976, she had almost nothing. She surrendered valuable marital assets to secure her freedom and retain the stage name under which she had become famous.

She was approaching 40, without the financial security her years of success should have provided.

The industry could easily have written her off.

Instead, she rebuilt her career and became an even greater star.

Judy Garland’s story offers another painful variation. Her life was marked by troubled marriages, financial instability and men who became involved in managing her career. But her addiction began long before those relationships, in a Hollywood studio system that exposed her to prescription drugs while she was still young. Her marriages compounded an already devastating struggle. By the end of her life, one of Hollywood’s greatest entertainers was facing serious financial hardship.

These women were not identical. Some endured abuse. Some struggled with addiction. Some faced financial exploitation. Some were failed by an entertainment industry that profited from their talents while offering little protection when their personal lives collapsed.

And that distinction matters.

It is tempting to look at a wedding photograph and declare that a woman chose the wrong man. It gives us a simple explanation for a complicated tragedy.

text:
If you called Florida's gambling addiction hotline anytime in the last year and a half, the guy running it was out on a $650,000 bond for stealing $1.4 million from his job to gamble.

He got almost 10 years in prison on Friday. And I'd bet hiring him actually made that hotline better.

Philip Sullivan was a CPA and the CFO of a property management company in Panama City. In April 2023 he started using the company card to buy gift cards and cash cards online, and all of it went to gambling. By then he'd already blown through his savings and taken out a bunch of personal loans. So once he was in the hole with the company's money too, he kept betting to try and win it back. Chasing your losses like that is literally one of the official symptoms doctors use to diagnose gambling addiction.

Over 11 months he took about $1.46 million, which works out to more than $4,000 a day. An internal audit finally caught it in March 2024, and he was arrested and fired.

Then he quit and went all in on recovery. A year after his arrest, with his case still pending, the Florida Council on Compulsive Gambling made him director of 888-ADMIT-IT. He says he talked to hundreds of people sitting in the same hole he'd dug for himself.

Addiction recovery has always run on people like him. Gamblers Anonymous has been run by gamblers since 1957. If you're a guy hiding $40,000 in credit card debt from your wife, you're going to open up a lot faster to someone who did the same thing with $1.4 million.

Psychiatrists used to count the stealing itself as a symptom. Until 2013, "forgery, fraud, theft, or embezzlement to finance gambling" was one of the ten official criteria in the DSM, the book doctors use to diagnose mental illness. They cut it from the new edition because it was redundant, since pretty much everyone who stole to gamble already qualified on the other criteria. Up to 40% of gamblers in treatment admit to committing crimes to pay for it.

So the judge in Bay County had a real mess to sort out on Friday. Sullivan's wife testified she watched his behavior change after he started taking Adderall. The company's controller testified he carefully worked his way around the fraud controls. And his own employer offers free legal help to people charged with gambling-related embezzlement, plus training for court staff on how addiction should factor into sentencing.

The judge gave him 118.5 months, and he went straight into custody. A podcast episode about his recovery had come out three days earlier.

Somewhere in Florida tonight, someone's staring at a company card they've already swiped too many times, trying to decide whether to call 888-ADMIT-IT. For the last year and a half, the guy in charge of that line knew exactly where that card leads.

text:
Jeff Bezos is worth about $365 billion, and he thinks AI will make it hard for companies like Amazon to find people who want to work.

He told Bret Baier on Fox News, standing on a Blue Origin factory floor in Florida: "Some people will decide, 'I can support my family working three days a week.' That's what productivity in the economy means."

Then came the line every hiring manager should sit with: "It's going to be difficult to hire people."

Here's what's going on.

Most of the loud voices in AI talk about job losses. Dario Amodei and Sam Altman have both warned about what the technology could do to workers. Bezos looked at the same forecasts and said, "I just happen to disagree with those smart people."

His bet is that AI lifts output per worker so much that many two-income households become one-income households by choice. One partner steps back while the other covers the bills. That shrinks the labor pool from the supply side.

The timing makes it interesting. Amazon has cut about 30,000 corporate roles since late 2025, and Bezos said headcount had swelled during the pandemic. The company plans to spend over $200 billion on capex this year, largely on data centers. So the founder is forecasting a tight labor market at the same moment his company runs with leaner corporate teams and far more machines.

We've heard a version of this before. In 1930, John Maynard Keynes wrote that his grandchildren's generation would enjoy a standard of living four to eight times higher and could get by on a fifteen-hour week. His deadline was 2030. We have four years left.

Henry Ford is the better precedent. In 1926 he moved his factory workers to a five-day, 40-hour week, partly because he believed people with free time would buy more of what factories made, cars included.

That's the real question for founders. If AI makes each employee far more productive, the scarce resource shifts from compute to people who still want to show up five days a week. The companies that win the next hiring cycle may be the ones that offer the shorter week first.

For investors, Bezos had a warning too. In a boom like this, he said, every experiment gets funded, the good ideas and the bad ideas, and in the moment it's hard to tell them apart.

One of the richest people alive is telling you to plan for a labor shortage. Build your hiring plan like he might be right.

text:
What made this documentary mesmerizing were the fourth-wall breaks. You realize that these aren’t characters, but actual people, and that not only are they deceiving each other, but they’re deceiving the documentary. They’re deceiving you. This is my attempt to make sense of it all.

Nathan Fielder brings comedic and creative genius, skillfully mixing a range of registers throughout the documentary. There were hilarious moments of total laughter that were grounded in serious themes, moments of relief only to be followed by mesmerizing segments you can’t take your eyes off, and pacing that at times felt monotonous but coalesced into deep realizations. The constant close-up face shots provoked countless questions of what each person was thinking at any given moment. Elizabeth’s soulless stares into Nathan as she defends herself from accusatory lines of questioning make you wonder if she’s deceiving you, the viewer, as much as she may be deceiving Nathan.

We get an intimate look into what it means to fall under Elizabeth’s thrall, as Nathan, to some degree, falls under it himself. Despite the irrefutable evidence of Elizabeth’s fraud, the documentary leaves viewers (and maybe even Nathan) with a lingering feeling that there’s more truth than meets the eye. Nathan himself is confused with how transparent Elizabeth and Billy are, even inviting him to live in their home. You can truly see everything. If these were really scam artists, why would they want such an intimate documentary following their life? Do they truly believe they’re in the right? Do they believe they can deceive the audience? Or do they simply believe that at least this way, they’ll at least become more humanized in the eyes of the public?

While it seems most people finished the documentary with a deeper sympathy for Elizabeth, I felt the opposite. I got a deeper look into how she attempts to pull people under her thrall, as she seemingly does with Nathan throughout the film. Near the start, when Nathan questions Elizabeth about how the device didn’t actually work she begins to cry and talks about her children. It’s impossible not to feel sympathy at this moment. You forget about the enormous pile of evidence against her, including everything she did admit to, and see her as a grieving mother of two kids who will soon be further away from her family than ever. This gives us a glimpse into what Elizabeth and Billy’s intention seems to be with the documentary. Instead of directly answering Nathan’s questions during this scene, Elizabeth stuns us with an emotional breakdown instead. While this reaction may have been completely genuine, knowing her history of deceit, it’s not implausible to assume the reaction was purposefully intentional to divert attention away from her crimes and towards humanizing her for the audience.

Nathan's questions during the documentary's interviews felt so banal that they shouldn't have worked, yet they consistently revealed insight into how Elizabeth and Billy approach the world both individually and together as a unit. This ultimately reveals a theme of control throughout the documentary. But it’s not Elizabeth controlling others; it’s Elizabeth being controlled by her partner Billy. Their "monuments of love" for each other, and the total trust and autonomy Elizabeth hands Billy over herself, build up as the movie goes on.

I saw the first instance revealing this dynamic near the start of the film when Elizabeth is whisking eggs while answering Nathan’s question, and Billy abruptly takes over for Elizabeth. Nathan immediately clocks this unusual move, asking Billy what was wrong with how Elizabeth was whisking the eggs. Fascinatingly, Billy and Elizabeth give different answers for why he took over. Billy tries to deflect by saying it’s because he wanted her to be able to focus on answering the questions. But Elizabeth offers up the real reason: she’s not beating the eggs right. I see this as a pivotal moment in the movie, because despite Elizabeth and Billy describing their relationship as a unit acting as one, this scene shows a sharp divergence in their immediate responses to Nathan’s confusion. One may think that Billy deflected simply because he didn’t want to come off overly-controlling of Elizabeth, but then, why would Elizabeth almost instinctually respond in a way that paints exactly that?

If the duo truly are as deeply connected as they say they are, Elizabeth would’ve gone along with Billy’s answer. However, I believe it’s possible Elizabeth saw this as a subtle opportunity to paint Billy as controlling without obviously coming off as intentionally trying to do so. Despite this being a documentary meant to capture transparency, not every line said by each person can be taken as transparent. Everyone has their incentives. Elizabeth can’t truly ever throw Billy under the bus on film, even if that’s what would be most authentic to her, because she knows he’s ultimately the only window she has to her kids. As the movie progresses, so does the theme of Billy being controlling. Nathan gives Elizabeth direct opportunities to comment on this, like when he asked her about being left out of the financial details Billy negotiated on her behalf for the documentary, but she never responded to these direct allegations. However, she indirectly said plenty. It’s possible she was deliberately painting a narrative with these subtle actions, and intentionally planted the seeds for Nathan to swing the theme of the documentary in this direction. After all, if she had never revealed the real reason Billy took over the eggs and had just played along with him, it’s possible this thematic direction would’ve never even taken place. Elizabeth wants you to feel that Nathan is the Director, and that the narratives presented in the movie are his choice, but her subtle actions seem to influence the film far more than Nathan can. Nathan falls under Elizabeth’s thrall without even realizing it; his documentary is hijacked.

Elizabeth’s reality distortion field is a theme that looms over the film throughout its running. Does she really not think she’s lying? During the segment when Nathan is questioning Elizabeth about the choice of words she used to describe Theranos’ technology, and how others can find it misleading, Elizabeth seems oblivious to how others may perceive her words differently than she does. I don’t buy her ignorance; it doesn’t take much intelligence to know how a claim of a machine currently being able to accomplish XYZ tasks insinuates that these tasks are already supported by the machine. I believe she feels the convenient angle to portray herself in during the documentary is one where she’s simply a misunderstood inventor who just wants to make the world a better place. Considering that she admitted to personally performing deceptions of all kinds, including forging pharmaceutical reports and covering up third-party machine use, Elizabeth is far from misunderstood. There was real intention behind her fraudulent actions. When Nathan asks her how she found herself in this situation, just weeks away from prison, she says she wishes she knew how. Of course she knows how, but coming off as misunderstood is simply convenient for her public image, and she plays the bit strikingly convincingly throughout the documentary. She paints herself as confused, lost, and the real victim in the controversy. Like the world is conspiring against her for no true reason.

What further reinforces this is how she handles Nathan’s hardest questions, often saying “I’m not sure” to questions that could be answered with a “yes” or “no”. Her biggest slip up here is when Elizabeth Holmes is on speakerphone and is asked if she knew Amanda Seyfried was in the room. Elizabeth replies with “I’m not sure if I knew.” What she seems to mean is “I’m not sure if saying I knew or I didn’t would be advantageous to me here.”

Bringing on Amanda Seyfried was probably the most impactful creative decision made for the film. We had a woman who played Elizabeth Holmes in the hit series The Dropout, now confronting the reality of the woman whose public reputation she directly helped tarnish but who she had never met. For scenes that couldn’t be recorded (like interactions between Nathan and Elizabeth in prison), Amanda was the one who did the re-enactments playing Elizabeth, at times even re-enacting scenes where Elizabeth referenced Amanda. Despite Amanda having played Elizabeth Holmes in her most critical and awards-sweeping role, she found herself, for the first time, truly in her sphere. When Nathan and Amanda visit Billy’s home in Texas together, Holmes calls from prison, and Billy puts her on speakerphone. Seyfried speaks with her briefly and cordially. This is the first and only time the two had spoken, since contact was strictly restricted during the production of The Dropout.

During the visit to Billy’s home, it doesn’t take long for Amanda and Billy to get into an argument. Billy reveals he controls Elizabeth’s Twitter account, which Amanda pushes back on, and the two get heated. Billy ridicules the irony of Amanda criticizing Billy’s control of Elizabeth’s social media presence, citing her recent backlash for her comments on Charlie Kirk, and it’s revealed Billy is a fan of Charlie Kirk. Interestingly, after the documentary comes out, the first thing that Billy tweets through Elizabeth’s Twitter account is a reply to a 2025 tweet from her (or more precisely, him) about Charlie Kirk’s words on forgiveness, to which he replied with “-EAH” (Elizabeth Anne Holmes). It’s odd that this is his first move. It’s been exposed that it’s you controlling Elizabeth’s Twitter account this whole time. Why bother to clarify that this specific tweet reflected her true thoughts? Perhaps with how Billy describes Elizabeth and him operating as one unit, if he’s going to be dragged for admitting his support of Charlie Kirk, he wanted Elizabeth to be dragged for it too.

While everything filmed in the documentary truly happened, it’s important to realize that Nathan is the one ultimately piecing the shots together, which carries great influence over the audience’s perception of everything going down. Multiple times throughout the documentary, Nathan stresses his commitment to ensuring its authenticity, and he deliberately crafts scenes to reinforce this commitment to us. For example, when Amanda is re-enacting scenes with Elizabeth, we see Nathan stop her to change things as simple as her tone of voice to truly portray the events honestly. There’s a particular scene where Nathan seems to think really hard over a specific word Elizabeth used to describe her level of awareness over Billy making financial negotiations regarding the documentary. He starts with thinking the word is “it”, but through going back and forth with Amanda, eventually decides the word she had actually used was “something”. These scenes are cleverly woven into the documentary to ensure the audience can trust Nathan’s journalistic integrity.

One of the smartest narratives crafted into the film calls directly to us, the audience. We’re made to feel complicit in even buying a ticket to the movie, when we learn that Billy negotiated a financial deal to get a cut of proceeds from the film’s success. Considering how narcissistic Billy comes off throughout the movie, the audience feels disgusted at putting money in Billy’s pocket. This skillfully makes the conflict feel larger than between the people in the film, but actually involves us as well. As Nathan threads making Elizabeth aware of Billy’s negotiation, we feel ourselves at stake right with him. After all, if there was a financial gain for Billy and Elizabeth from the film diminishing the documentary’s integrity, how much of what we had just watched could we even trust? As the movie ends, we learn that Billy ultimately gave up a financial interest in the film, leaving us with an ending of relief.

But perhaps the greatest deception in the documentary is the illusion that we've finally escaped it. We're relieved to learn that Billy isn’t profiting from the film, reassured by Nathan's consistent commitment to authenticity, and left believing that we've seen through Elizabeth's attempts to manipulate us. Yet all of these feelings are themselves products of a narrative deliberately constructed for us. Nathan decides what we see, what we don't, and ultimately what we walk away believing. Elizabeth, meanwhile, may have exercised far more influence over that narrative than either Nathan or the audience realizes. The documentary leaves us questioning who was deceiving whom, but perhaps the more fascinating question is who was really in control. Nathan set out to document a woman who deceived the world, only to create a film in which we're never quite sure whether we're watching him expose her deception, or watching her deceive him into telling the story she wanted told.

text:
The day I met my partner, we were at Zijing Sports Field. It was the day after my graduation ceremony. Seeing me already completely wasted after just half a bottle of Japanese sake bought from Tmall Supermarket, she offered a piece of philosophy: “When life trips me up, I fire up a barbecue right where I fall.”

I loved her wit and her way of looking at life. There seemed to be something deeply thoughtful beneath that absurd remark. It applies to my work and life, too. I run into walls all the time. Life trips me up, and sometimes I stay down and have a barbecue. But many other times, I want to push back, to actively change things, to take what I can change and make something more of it, then share it with others who need it.

The same goes for open source. I often discover that I need something, and that an open-source project already exists to meet that need. Only after trying it myself do I find the gaps. Fortunately, I am still young. I shouldn't just leave those needs unmet. This is one place where I can't simply settle down for a barbecue.

A few months ago, Xuesong told me how incredibly useful voice input had become. Anyone who has actually worked with me knows that I am anything but aloof. If anything, I tend to get carried away and talk too much. Voice input lets me dump the scattered thoughts in my head several times faster, dramatically increasing how quickly I can get them out. I soon tried an open-source voice input app called Voxt and fell in love with it. Yes, Voxt is now part of the SGLang Omni ecosystem, and we get to keep improving it alongside its creator, Guan Wei. But let me go back to when I first tried it, about half a year ago. The idea was simple: use MLX Audio to serve an ASR model that transcribes speech into user input, then pass that input to an LLM to polish according to instructions.

After a day of using it, I noticed something odd about the latency of Qwen ASR + Qwen3 4B. My intuition told me that even with MLX LLM serving Qwen3 4B, a model this small shouldn't be that slow. A closer look revealed that the original Voxt team had assembled the prompt in the wrong order. To reuse the KV cache, the order should be system prompt + user input. But Voxt was sending user input + system prompt to the LLM. I immediately submitted my first PR. I wanted faster input. I liked open-source software. Of course it wasn't perfect, and I didn't know my way around the Swift stack.

Still, it seemed that if we worked on it together, these difficulties were things we could overcome. Life doesn't always go smoothly. There are plenty of things I can accept, places where I can stay down and have a barbecue. But at least when it comes to open-source software, I want to try submitting a PR.

That was how my story with Voxt began: another story of a user with an unmet need becoming a developer.

A few days ago, we released Voxt 0.16. It is an honor to build such an excellent local voice input system alongside Guan Wei. ASR now runs on SGLang Omni MLX, and the LLM polishing stage will soon run within the SGLang MLX ecosystem as well.

As it happens, my story with SGLang also began with a transition from user to developer. In August 2024, I was working on a project that combined embedding-based retrieval with LLM agent memory tree search. Looking back, those were still the frontier days of LLM inference. My experiments always felt slow. Then one afternoon, I came across an introduction to SGLang in Synced. The moment I saw “Radix Tree for KV Cache,” something clicked. How could a design be this clever? Wasn't this exactly the system my agent tree search needed?

I switched to SGLang without hesitation, and my agents did indeed run much faster. There was one catch: running eight Llama 8B instances on eight GPUs didn't seem quite so trivial. Sending requests at random to arbitrary GPUs didn't seem optimal. At the time, I didn't even know what a DP rank was, or what round-robin meant. But that didn't matter. I wanted speed. Clever me—actually, a complete novice in the inference world—quickly figured that if requests from the same agent went to the same DP rank whenever possible, KV cache reuse should improve considerably.

Meanwhile, I discovered that SGLang couldn't yet serve the embedding model I needed. Running two separate inference frameworks was a hassle, so I put together an implementation that supported my model.

With those two ideas in mind, I emailed Ying and Lianmin, also hoping I might get a chance to learn from these two professors who were about to join UCLA. Well, as you can probably tell, that was how everything began.

What I remember is that inference infrastructure was hard to use, but I needed it. I didn't want to leave my experiments crawling along. I wanted to change something within my reach, and perhaps do everything I could to reach a little further.

What prompted all this writing was a small incident today while we were making demos of SGLang Omni's full-duplex capabilities. If you read the blog post, you'll see the clear, polished demos recorded by two handsome young men on our team, Wenyao and Jeffro. The open-source software they used to record and edit those demos was Recordly. To get the recordings right, Wenyao fixed two critical bugs in it.

We joked in the group chat: “Wenyao could submit a PR to Recordly now.”

“At least two.”

I said, quite seriously, yes, he absolutely should. Then I shared how, with both Voxt and SGLang, I had gone from a user tripped up by life to a developer trying to push back.

The story continues. People's needs keep changing. Open-source software always has problems, and countless needs remain unmet. Life trips us up again and again. I've come to accept that. After all, barbecue tastes pretty good. I started writing this on a plane. I've landed now, and I'm about to go have barbecue with my colleagues.

But when we can, we'll keep pushing back, trying to get back on our feet in the mud. Tripped up again and again, still hoping we can make things better.

text:
If you're young, why aren't you joining a rocket ship instead of starting an agency?

I agree with Nick here.

At ColdIQ, I think we've had 9 agencies spin out from ex-employees.

I think a lot of them thought they'd have 50K or 100K of profit in their pocket.

But that's not the reality.

You have a lot of people with starving businesses.

They work super hard. They work 16-hour days to make less than they would at a great tech company.

There are a few agencies that make above 100K. A lot more make below that and can't really scale past 20 or 30K.

For now there's a lot of concentration in the best companies. They're growing so fast that it's much better to join a rocket ship than trying to run a service business.

I have a good example.

One of my best friends joined one of the best AI companies in Germany as a founding AI engineer.

He got around 1% equity. Three years later he's a millionaire.

He didn't take the risk of starting a business. And he made an amazing salary while getting there.

That would actually be my recommendation as well:

→ Find a job at a super fast-growing company.
→ Offer to do the work for free to get your foot in the door.
→ Show them you can do the thing you're pitching, with proof you've done it before.

Even if it's less than 1% equity, I think it's a much higher chance of becoming extremely wealthy.

So for me, if you don't have an edge, and you usually don't when you start your career, I think it's much better to work for a fast-growing tech company than to launch your own agency.

Even more now that judgment and experience are going to be the commodity that companies are paying you for.

When you're young, you don't have any judgment.

So you need to learn somewhere before you try to sell your judgment and make a profit out of it.

I think a lot of young people want to be an entrepreneur because it's very glamorized. But I don't think it's the best path to wealth.

Foreign shoots generate around $1 billion annually for the province. 
However, Quebec's true financial and critical success comes from its dual-threat model: acting as a premium service provider to Hollywood while simultaneously fostering a highly lucrative domestic market. 

The province "cleans up" financially and culturally through several key pillars:
1. The Language Barrier as a Financial Shield
In English Canada, local films face fierce, direct box-office competition from multi-million-dollar American blockbusters. 

Quebec has a built-in cultural defense. 
Because the primary language is French, the province has cultivated its own star system, celebrity ecosystem, and massive public demand for homegrown content.

Users on Reddit point out a massive point of consensus: Quebec-made films regularly beat out massive Hollywood blockbusters at the local box office. 
For instance, Quebec films often capture a massive share of provincial ticket sales, a feat unmatched anywhere else in North America. 

This cultural sovereignty translates directly into massive box office revenues that stay within the province.

2. Global Leader in Visual Effects (VFX) and Post-Production
While places like Alberta and British Columbia compete fiercely to host physical movie sets, Quebec has quietly captured the highly technical back-end of Hollywood. 

According to Statistics Canada, Quebec is Canada's absolute juggernaut in post-production, accounting for 52.1% of national operating revenue in the sector—topping $1.4 billion.

Montreal has become one of the top three global hubs for animation and VFX. 

Even if Hollywood films a movie in Atlanta or London, there is a massive chance the digital dinosaurs, explosions, or sci-fi environments are engineered by a tech studio in Montreal. 

To keep this going, Quebec offers a base all-spend credit of 25% with an additional 16% bonus explicitly for computer-aided animation and special effects labor. 

3. Architecture as a Global Stand-In

Physically, Montreal and Quebec City offer Hollywood something no other location in North America can seamlessly provide: believable European locations. 

With its historic cobblestone streets, centuries-old stone buildings, and European flair, Quebec frequently doubles for Paris, London, or historic New York at a fraction of the cost. 

Massive blockbusters like Transformers: 
Rise of the Beasts and high-profile streaming series like Amazon's Three Pines have utilized the province's unique aesthetic. 

4. Recent Friction in the Market
Despite its massive success, Quebec's industry is navigating a few economic speed bumps:

Tax Credit Ceilings: 
To manage the provincial budget, the Quebec government implemented a 65% cap on eligible production expenses for certain tech tax credits. 

Local VFX and animation studios have raised alarms, stating that this cost control has caused them to narrowly lose a few high-profile Hollywood contracts to more aggressive regions. 

Linguistic Shifts: 
While the French-language side thrives, CTV News Montreal reported that local English-language crews and actors have felt a squeeze, as provincial incentives are heavily focused on French-language cultural preservation.

Ultimately, Quebec proved to the film world that you don't just have to be a passive playground for American studios. 

By using Hollywood money to fund state-of-the-art tech infrastructure, Quebec built a resilient model that feeds its own culture while collecting massive financial checks from the U.S. studio system.
