Last week’s falling-out between Ukrainian President Zelensky and the American president has left me torn. Trump has not only started buying Russian diesel directly, he has also said that Ukraine should change its president. Zelensky said that America now stands on the side of the aggressor, and told Europe’s leaders to their faces that they are the “real leaders.”
Without America’s support, what is Ukraine to do?
Zelensky had to lay his cards on the table for Europe’s “real leaders”: if Ukraine loses, Europe will have to take in twenty million Ukrainian refugees; if the fighting continues, next year’s war will have a funding gap of 70 billion euros.
Faced with his request, the “real leaders” didn’t exactly rise to the occasion. They actually didn’t agree, and said they needed to study it further!
What the hell is there to study? The EU’s GDP in 2025 is nearly 19 trillion euros. What is another 70 billion to resist the Russian aggressor?
Watching the “real leaders” hesitate, wanting to say something but holding back, Zelensky immediately named Canada, Japan and Australia, hoping they too would put up a bit more money.
Faced with Zelensky asking for money yet again, I, as an Australian taxpayer, am torn. I have three worries:
First, if I help him raise another 70 billion, will Ukraine definitely defeat Russia next year? If it doesn’t, how much will be needed the year after?
Second, if the war goes on, could someone blow up a nuclear power plant, or even use nuclear weapons? The recorded history of humankind shows again and again that in war, people have never been sparing with the most advanced weapons: if they have knives, they use knives; if they have guns, they use guns; if they have poison gas, they use poison gas; if they have nuclear bombs, they use nuclear bombs.
Third, Australia’s economy is in poor shape now, and a major reason is the high price of oil. The world’s energy production capacity sits in one single pool. From the very start, this war blew up Europe’s gas pipelines, and now Ukraine has begun bombing Russia’s gas and oil facilities. If the fighting continues, oil in Australia will surely get ever more expensive. If we keep giving money, our economy will get worse. And what are the consequences of a bad economy? Melbourne’s economy is struggling, and this city, billed as the world’s most livable, now has terrible public safety. France’s economy is poor too. Last week there were riots there, and many shopping centres, restaurants, cars and police stations were burned.
I believe these three worries must also be the worries of the “real leaders.” Being torn makes people cautious. So I began to study this war, which has now lasted longer than the First World War, to find out what it is really about.
The Soviet Union dissolved in 1991, and Ukraine became independent the same year and began to elect its own presidents. At independence, seven regions in Ukraine’s east and south, plus the capital Kyiv, were mainly Russian-speaking. These eight Russian-speaking areas were the engine of Ukraine’s economy, and its seaports and main industries were concentrated there.
For reasons I can’t quite fathom, independent Ukraine suffered from severe corruption and a weak economy. The people were discontented and changed presidents often. In 2010 they elected a pro-Russian president. In 2014, a section of the people, unhappy with his drift toward Russia, drove him from office by force (Ukraine calls it the “Revolution of Dignity”; Russia calls it an “illegal uprising”), and he fled to Russia. This is exactly what Putin keeps repeating: that today’s Ukrainian government is illegitimate because it was founded on violence, not democracy.
Putin’s complaints don’t stop there. After independence, Ukraine gradually restricted the use of Russian. After the 2014 revolution the restrictions grew tighter: soldiers, civil servants, doctors and teachers were required to use Ukrainian, and schools were no longer allowed to teach in Russian.
Among these wealthy Russian-speaking regions, the share of Russian speakers was highest in Crimea, at 97%, and lowest in Mykolaiv Oblast, at 66%. After independence, people in these regions grew increasingly resentful and held referendums that were illegal. Why illegal? Because Ukraine’s constitution says that to become independent, all Ukrainians must vote together; the Russian-speaking regions cannot decide on their own. But the people of Crimea ignored this and voted to join Russia, so Putin, for whom blood is thicker than water, took Crimea back in one stroke.
The other Russian-speaking regions in the east and south saw the example and followed it. They not only held referendums but also raised their own armed forces and seized government buildings. The Ukrainian army used force and suppressed the separatism in most places, but some areas have remained under pro-Russian armed groups.
I believe there must be a Russian hand behind the unrest in these regions. But the hidden hand is not only Russia’s. Some say the hand that drove the legitimate pro-Russian president from power was America’s, and they point as evidence to footage of Americans, after the coup succeeded, training Ukrainian police in how to keep order and teaching Ukrainians how to prevent corruption.
Facing this mess, the comedian Zelensky was elected president in 2019 by a landslide. As soon as he took office, he actively sought to join NATO, hoping for Western military protection.
Putin saw this and lost his temper: if Ukraine joined NATO, NATO troops could march right up to Russia’s border. So in 2022 Putin struck first and launched his “special military operation.”
Yesterday, Zelensky, in front of television audiences around the world, said with great hurt: we have been betrayed by America.
Ukraine has indeed been betrayed by America. Trump has not only started buying Russian diesel, he has also throttled the speed of the satellite internet that Ukraine’s military relies on so heavily, and halted other sanctions on Russia.
Zelensky looked miserable on television. How could he not? Ukraine has become what it is today under his leadership. This is not the first time America has betrayed Ukraine. In 1994, Ukraine was the world’s third-largest nuclear power. When it decided to give up its nuclear weapons, it was America and the West that pushed it to do so. The United States, Britain and Russia signed the Budapest Memorandum, pledging that if Ukraine gave up its nuclear weapons, they would respect Ukraine’s sovereignty and borders and safeguard its security.
Yet in 2014, Russia seized Crimea with barely a shot fired, and America and the West did not fire a single shot in response! If that isn’t betrayal, what is?!
This puzzles me: why didn’t America and the West support Ukraine in fighting Russia in 2014 the way they do now? And why didn’t Ukraine, equally losing territory, fight Russia to the death in 2014 as it does now?
I suspect there is something unspoken behind this. Perhaps it was this very thing that let Putin taste success, and so we have today’s Ukraine: a population down by 20 million, 20% of its territory lost, its economy largely destroyed, and more than a million dead or wounded.
What is this unspoken thing? I don’t know.
What I do know is this: the American president who promised in 1994 to protect Ukraine’s security was Clinton; the American president when Russia seized Crimea in 2014 was Obama; the American president who gave Ukraine money and weapons in 2022 was Biden; and the American president who now doesn’t support Ukraine fighting on is Trump.
Which of them represents America?
Zelensky’s grievance is ultimately because he is too young. He doesn’t understand America, doesn’t understand the West, doesn’t understand human nature.
When Putin was young, he didn’t understand America and the West either. He was 47 when he took office, and he wanted to join NATO. The Soviet Union had only recently collapsed, and he felt the West was stronger, more advanced and richer than Russia, so he wanted in. His thinking was simple: as a NATO member, Russia would not only gain NATO’s protection but could also concentrate on its economy. He offered a warm face and got a cold shoulder: NATO didn’t want Russia. Putin understood at once that the West saw Russia as an enemy, and so Russia had to maintain strong military power.
Moreover, since the war began, Putin has repeatedly said that Russia was betrayed by America, because when the Soviet Union dissolved, America, on NATO’s behalf, promised Russia verbally that NATO would not expand eastward and would not pose a military threat to Russian territory. Yet in 2019 Ukraine wrote its aim of joining NATO into its constitution, openly courting the alliance. Putin’s view is that Ukraine could never have done this without America’s tacit approval.
I dug further and found a 2013 CNN video in which former U.S. President Bill Clinton is interviewed by Piers Morgan, on Piers Morgan Live, broadcast in September 2013. Morgan asked whether Putin had ever broken a private agreement. Clinton answered: “No, he did not.” And: “He kept his word in all of the deals we made.” Clinton also described their relationship as “brutally blunt.” He was speaking of the period around 2000, when the two men overlapped in office.
Digging further still, I found that in June 2001, at a joint press conference in Slovenia after meeting Putin, the American president at the time, George W. Bush, said something that went down in history: “I looked the man in the eye. I found him very straightforward and trustworthy … I was able to get a sense of his soul.”
Having come this far, I know I cannot possibly get to the bottom of the causes of the Ukraine-Russia war, let alone judge who is right and who is wrong. But I know one thing: if the fighting goes on, more people will die, the economy will get worse, and Sydney’s public safety will end up like France’s. Worst of all, it could lead to nuclear war.
So, as a selfish Australian taxpayer, I no longer want to support Ukraine.
Unfortunately, last month Australia added another A$15 million in aid for Ukraine, and so far Australian taxpayers have thrown A$1.9 billion of firewood onto this Ukraine-Russia fire.
I hear that the Australian prime minister has more than 60 advisers on taxpayer-funded salaries. They can’t possibly be unaware of what I have set out here. If they do know, why do they keep letting the prime minister spend taxpayers’ money pouring oil on the fire?
Could it really be as the conspiracy theory says, that the West wants to use the Ukraine-Russia war to eliminate Russia, the greatest threat to world peace?
If so, Ukraine has truly become the sucker among mercenaries: fighting all these years, losing so much territory, so many lives, without bringing Russia down, while its Western paymasters are starting to lose their nerve!
Who should bear responsibility for the Ukraine-Russia war? Putin, who struck first, is certainly not blameless, but is he the only one responsible? Do the Ukrainians who restricted Russian-language schooling for children whose mother tongue is Russian bear no responsibility? Do the Western voters who keep sending Ukraine money bear none?
Whether in East or West, education, the media, history books, films and literature all cast “betrayal” (breaking promises, treachery, ingratitude, defection…) as immoral, so that when people are accused of “betrayal,” they blush. But anyone who has lived past seventy, East or West, comes to understand that most betrayals in this world are done out of necessity.
Betrayal and deception are not the same thing. Deception is knowing the outcome in advance and deliberately deceiving someone. Betrayal is making a promise without knowing its consequences, and abandoning it when you discover you cannot bear them.
C. S. Lewis made the same point about a wrong road: the person who turns back soonest is the one truly making progress.
To help my two granddaughters and their descendants navigate this conflict-ridden world and stay as safe and wise as possible, I wrote this book recommending fourteen must-read titles, including C.S. Lewis’s Mere Christianity.

I believe these three worries must also be the worries of the “real leaders.” Being torn makes people cautious. So I began to study this war, which has now lasted longer than the First World War, to find out what it is really about.
The Soviet Union dissolved in 1991, and Ukraine became independent the same year and began to elect its own presidents. At independence, seven regions in Ukraine’s east and south, plus the capital Kyiv, were mainly Russian-speaking. These eight Russian-speaking areas were the engine of Ukraine’s economy, and its seaports and main industries were concentrated there.
For reasons I can’t quite fathom, independent Ukraine suffered from severe corruption and a weak economy. The people were discontented and changed presidents often. In 2010 they elected a pro-Russian president. In 2014, a section of the people, unhappy with his drift toward Russia, drove him from office by force (Ukraine calls it the “Revolution of Dignity”; Russia calls it an “illegal uprising”), and he fled to Russia. This is exactly what Putin keeps repeating: that today’s Ukrainian government is illegitimate because it was founded on violence, not democracy.
Putin’s complaints don’t stop there. After independence, Ukraine gradually restricted the use of Russian. After the 2014 revolution the restrictions grew tighter: soldiers, civil servants, doctors and teachers were required to use Ukrainian, and schools were no longer allowed to teach in Russian.
Among these wealthy Russian-speaking regions, the share of Russian speakers was highest in Crimea, at 97%, and lowest in Mykolaiv Oblast, at 66%. After independence, people in these regions grew increasingly resentful and held referendums that were illegal. Why illegal? Because Ukraine’s constitution says that to become independent, all Ukrainians must vote together; the Russian-speaking regions cannot decide on their own. But the people of Crimea ignored this and voted to join Russia, so Putin, for whom blood is thicker than water, took Crimea back in one stroke.

The Ukrainian army used force and suppressed the separatism in most places, but some areas have remained under pro-Russian armed groups.
I believe there must be a Russian hand behind the unrest in these regions. But the hidden hand is not only Russia’s. Some say the hand that drove the legitimate pro-Russian president from power was America’s, and they point as evidence to footage of Americans, after the coup succeeded, training Ukrainian police in how to keep order and teaching Ukrainians how to prevent corruption.
Facing this mess, the comedian Zelensky was elected president in 2019 by a landslide. As soon as he took office, he actively sought to join NATO, hoping for Western military protection.
Putin saw this and lost his temper: if Ukraine joined NATO, NATO troops could march right up to Russia’s border. So in 2022 Putin struck first and launched his “special military operation.”
Yesterday, Zelensky, in front of television audiences around the world, said with great hurt: we have been betrayed by America.
Ukraine has indeed been betrayed by America. Trump has not only started buying Russian diesel, he has also throttled the speed of the satellite internet that Ukraine’s military relies on so heavily, and halted other sanctions on Russia.
Zelensky looked miserable on television. How could he not? Ukraine has become what it is today under his leadership. This is not the first time America has betrayed Ukraine. In 1994, Ukraine was the world’s third-largest nuclear power. When it decided to give up its nuclear weapons, it was America and the West that pushed it to do so. The United States, Britain and Russia signed the Budapest Memorandum, pledging that if Ukraine gave up its nuclear weapons, they would respect Ukraine’s sovereignty and borders and safeguard its security.
Yet in 2014, Russia seized Crimea with barely a shot fired, and America and the West did not fire a single shot in response! If that isn’t betrayal, what is?!
This puzzles me: why didn’t America and the West support Ukraine in fighting Russia in 2014 the way they do now? And why didn’t Ukraine, equally losing territory, fight Russia to the death in 2014 as it does now?
I suspect there is something unspoken behind this. Perhaps it was this very thing that let Putin taste success, and so we have today’s Ukraine: a population down by 20 million, 20% of its territory lost, its economy largely destroyed, and more than a million dead or wounded.
What is this unspoken thing? I don’t know.
What I do know is this: the American president who promised in 1994 to protect Ukraine’s security was Clinton; the American president when Russia seized Crimea in 2014 was Obama; the American president who gave Ukraine money and weapons in 2022 was Biden; and the American president who now doesn’t support Ukraine fighting on is Trump.

Zelensky’s grievance is ultimately because he is too young. He doesn’t understand America, doesn’t understand the West, doesn’t understand human nature.
When Putin was young, he didn’t understand America and the West either. He was 47 when he took office, and he wanted to join NATO. The Soviet Union had only recently collapsed, and he felt the West was stronger, more advanced and richer than Russia, so he wanted in. His thinking was simple: as a NATO member, Russia would not only gain NATO’s protection but could also concentrate on its economy. He offered a warm face and got a cold shoulder: NATO didn’t want Russia. Putin understood at once that the West saw Russia as an enemy, and so Russia had to maintain strong military power.

text:
Good morning from Virginia. 🇺🇸

On an ordinary October morning in 1803, the United States Senate gathered in the unfinished Capitol and voted to approve a treaty that would forever change the shape of the nation. The Louisiana Purchase had been signed in Paris that spring by Robert Livingston and James Monroe, two American envoys who had gone to France expecting only to bargain for New Orleans and the rights of deposit along the Mississippi. Instead they found themselves face to face with Napoleon Bonaparte, a man whose attention had turned elsewhere. France had lost Saint-Domingue to a successful slave revolt, the cost of holding the vast Louisiana Territory had grown unattractive, and the First Consul needed cash for the armies he intended to send against Britain. In a matter of days the Americans were offered the entire territory—roughly 828,000 square miles stretching from the Gulf of Mexico to the northern plains, and from the Mississippi River to the distant Rockies—for fifteen million dollars.

Thomas Jefferson, who had spent his public life arguing for a strict reading of the Constitution, now faced a decision that seemed to stretch the document past recognition. He fretted over the legality of the purchase in private letters even as he recognized its necessity. Western farmers and traders depended on the free passage of the river; without New Orleans in American hands, the settlements beyond the Appalachians could drift away from the Union or fall under foreign control. The Senate debate reflected those tensions. Federalists warned that the new land would dilute the power of the original states and create a republic too large to govern. Republicans answered that the river was the lifeblood of the West and that the alternative—war with France or endless diplomatic uncertainty—was far more dangerous. On October 20 the treaty passed by a vote of 24 to 7.

The territory itself remained largely a blank on American maps. Spanish officials still occupied New Orleans until the formal transfer could be arranged. Native nations had lived across the region for generations, and no American could yet say with certainty what lay beyond the Mississippi’s western bank. Within weeks Jefferson would commission Meriwether Lewis and William Clark to lead a small party of soldiers, hunters, and boatmen up the Missouri River and across the unknown country to the Pacific. The purchase had not only doubled the nation’s land; it had opened a continent whose rivers, mountains, and plains would shape American life for the next century. In a single Senate vote the young republic stepped from the banks of the Mississippi toward a future no one in the room could fully imagine.

DON ’T BELIEVE THE POLLS - REPUBLICANS CAN WIN!
Don’t believe the polls! Many are designed to make Republicans feel there is no reason to vote.
Anyone can conduct a poll solely to obtain specific results and have it picked up by supposedly reliable sources. In

That was a doublespeak way of saying, “we lied.”

specifically designed to lead people toward a desired result. Even supposedly reputable polling companies often have
some push poll objectives. FormPlus explains how push polls work:
Leading Questions: Instead of phrasing questions neutrally like “Do you support Candidate A?”, a push
poll would ask, “Would you support Candidate A if you knew they increased tuition fee by 250%, making
tertiary education unaffordable?”
False or Misleading Claims: Some push polls not only steer opinions but also include outright lies (e.g.,

text:
“Then, because so many people were coming and going that they did not even have a chance to eat, he said to them, ‘Come with me by yourselves to a quiet place and get some rest.’” — Mark 6:31

Over the Balsam Mountains from Kuwohi (Clingmans Dome), Great Smoky Mountains National Park, North Carolina and Tennessee, USA.

The disciples had just come back from their first big mission. Jesus had sent them out two by two into the villages, and they returned bursting with stories of people healed and hearts turned toward God. But the crowds never let up. People kept arriving and leaving, needs kept piling up, and the friends of Jesus were so busy they had not even sat down to eat. Jesus noticed. Before He asked them for anything more, He invited them to come away with Him and rest.

They climbed into a boat and headed for a quiet spot, but the crowd ran ahead along the shore and was waiting when they landed. Instead of sighing, Jesus looked at all those people with compassion, because they were like sheep without a shepherd. He taught them until evening. Then He took five small loaves and two fish, gave thanks, and kept breaking the bread. More than five thousand people ate until they were satisfied, and the tired disciples gathered twelve full baskets of leftovers. The same Lord who cared about their rest also made sure there was more than enough for everyone, including them.

That invitation is still open. Jesus is not impressed by how little sleep you got or how full your calendar looks. He sees the nurse finishing a double shift, the parent who has not had a quiet minute since sunrise, the student juggling work and classes, the caregiver who keeps pouring out for someone else. Rest is not a reward you earn after everything is done. It is a gift He offers in the middle of the busyness, because He knows you were never meant to run on empty.

So this Tuesday, take Him up on it. Step outside for ten unhurried minutes. Eat a real meal without a screen. Turn off the phone a little earlier tonight and let your mind settle. And if you see someone who is running ragged, give them a little room to breathe: cover a task, bring a coffee, tell them it is okay to slow down. Like these blue ridges folding quietly into one another for miles, His peace stretches farther than your to-do list, and there is always more than enough grace to carry you through.

Dated 3 May 2025, the message reads: “Once the money comes to the company here, I will arrange the donation to Kennedy Centre [sic], and you'll be joining the VIP events and get close with the administration, even with POTUS.”

According to reports by Axios and NYT, Mildon wired roughly $17.6 million to a Houston-based Texas Armament & Technology (TX-AT), with about $5.6 to $6 million intended as a donation for the Kennedy Center.

Mildon’s wife later confronted President Donald Trump in the Oval Office, alleging that the multi-million-dollar donation never reached the Kennedy Center and that Grenell offered political access and VIP proximity in exchange for financial backing. The texts also touched upon business ties involving Venezuela.

Grenell has strongly denied sending the text message, dismissed the allegations as "absurd" and "lies", and stated he never solicited or received funds from Mildon.

It looks like the Mildon money was creamed off at some stage - but where and by whom?

Magnifica Air is developing a new category of luxury air travel that sits between traditional First Class and private aviation.

The Florida-based company plans to launch in 2027 using specially configured Airbus A220-300 and A321neo aircraft.

Its first A220 is now in production, while the airline is expanding its recruitment efforts ahead of operations.

A conventional A220-300 typically accommodates 120–160 passengers.

Magnifica plans to carry just 45–54 guests per aircraft, creating considerably more room for individual seating, privacy and onboard service.

The A220 will feature two private suites, while the larger A321neo will offer four.

Luxury aircraft specialist Comlux is responsible for the custom cabin interiors, including seating, connectivity and bespoke design elements.

The experience is intended to begin before passengers board.

Magnifica plans to use private terminals, with arrivals just 30 minutes before departure, dedicated security screening and personalized baggage handling.

Onboard, passengers can expect premium dining, spacious seating and hospitality inspired by private aviation.

Initial routes are planned between major American cities, including Miami, New York, Los Angeles, Dallas and Houston.

The airline is currently preparing for its 2027 debut rather than operating scheduled flights.

For travellers who appreciate private aviation but don’t need to charter an entire aircraft, Magnifica is attempting to create an entirely different way to fly.

text:
On October 20, 1803: The U.S. Senate Ratifies the Louisiana Purchase

On October 20, 1803, the United States Senate approved for ratification the treaty by which the young American republic acquired the vast Louisiana Territory from France. By a vote of 24 to 7, the Senate endorsed a deal that roughly doubled the size of the United States overnight and opened the door to westward expansion across the continent.

The territory, stretching from the Mississippi River to the Rocky Mountains and from the Gulf of Mexico toward the Canadian border, encompassed approximately 828,000 square miles—an area larger than the combined size of Great Britain, France, Germany, Italy, Spain, and Portugal at the time. It would eventually form all or part of 15 states, including Louisiana, Arkansas, Missouri, Iowa, Oklahoma, Kansas, Nebraska, the Dakotas, and portions of Minnesota, New Mexico, Montana, Wyoming, and Colorado. 

The Road to the Bargain
Control of the Mississippi River and the port of New Orleans had long been a vital interest for American settlers west of the Appalachians, whose agricultural exports depended on free navigation of the river. Spain had held Louisiana since 1762. In 1800, under pressure from Napoleon Bonaparte, Spain secretly agreed to retrocede the territory to France via the Treaty of San Ildefonso. 

President Thomas Jefferson, alarmed by the prospect of a powerful French presence astride the Mississippi, dispatched Robert R. Livingston (the U.S. minister to France) and later James Monroe to negotiate. Their original instructions authorized them to spend up to about $10 million for New Orleans and adjacent territory in the Floridas. Jefferson famously wrote that the day France took possession of New Orleans, the United States “must marry ourselves to the British fleet and nation.” 

Events in Europe and the Caribbean shifted the calculus. Napoleon’s plans for a North American empire faltered amid the Haitian Revolution, the failure to reconquer Saint-Domingue, and the looming renewal of war with Britain. Rather than risk losing Louisiana to the British Royal Navy and gaining nothing, Napoleon decided to sell the entire territory. French officials surprised the American negotiators by offering not just New Orleans but all of Louisiana. 

On April 30, 1803 (the treaty was signed May 2 and backdated), Livingston and Monroe agreed to the purchase for $15 million: $11.25 million in cash (to be paid via bonds) plus assumption of $3.75 million in American claims against France. The effective price worked out to roughly three to four cents per acre—one of history’s greatest real-estate bargains. Napoleon later remarked that the acquisition would give England “a maritime rival that sooner or later will lay low her pride.” 

Jefferson’s Constitutional Dilemma and the Senate Vote
Jefferson, a strict constructionist who believed the Constitution limited federal powers to those explicitly enumerated, privately worried that nothing in the document clearly authorized the purchase of foreign territory. He considered proposing a constitutional amendment but ultimately concluded that delay risked Napoleon withdrawing the offer. As he noted privately, “The less we say about constitutional difficulties the better.” Supporters argued that the power to govern territory implied the power to acquire it; the Senate and later the Supreme Court effectively accepted this pragmatic reading. 

After the treaty reached Washington, Jefferson submitted it to the Senate. Debate lasted two days. Federalist opponents, outnumbered, objected to what they saw as executive overreach without clear constitutional sanction and fretted that distant settlements might weaken loyalty to the Union. On October 20 the Senate voted 24–7 in favor. Jefferson ratified the treaty the next day, and the United States moved quickly to take possession.

Warangal Police Commissioner N. Sweta, IPS, Performs Ayudha Pooja at Police Headquarters

Special Worship Conducted for Police Weapons and Vehicles on Vijayadashami; Commissioner Extends Festive Greetings to the Public and Police Personnel

Warangal: On the occasion of Vijayadashami, Warangal Police Commissioner N. Sweta, IPS, performed traditional Ayudha Pooja at the Warangal Police Headquarters on Tuesday. She extended her heartfelt Vijayadashami greetings to the public, police officers, personnel, and their family members.

On Tuesday morning, special prayers were conducted at the temple in the armory at the Police Headquarters in the presence of Goddess Durga, under the guidance of Vedic scholars. The Police Commissioner, along with senior police officers, participated in the traditional rituals marking Vijayadashami, which symbolizes the victory of good over evil.

Subsequently, special worship was performed for police vehicles in coordination with personnel from the Armed Reserve Police Wing and the Motor Transport Department. Special prayers were also offered to the Jammi tree as part of the Vijayadashami celebrations.

Speaking on the occasion, Commissioner N. Sweta wished that people across the Warangal Police Commissionerate limits would celebrate the festival with devotion, joy, and enthusiasm in a peaceful atmosphere.

She stated that the police department works tirelessly, day and night, to maintain law and order and ensure a peaceful environment for the public. Emphasizing the importance of weapons in police operations, she noted that performing special worship for weapons on Vijayadashami is a longstanding tradition.

The Commissioner expressed hope that the auspicious festival would bring happiness, success, and prosperity into everyone's lives.

Police Officials Who Participated

The programme was attended by East Zone DCP Ankit Kumar, Central Zone DCP Dhara Kavitha, Additional DCP (Administration) Royal Prabhakar Rao, Additional DCP (Crimes) Balaswami, Armed Reserve Additional DCPs Suresh and Srinivas, Armed Reserve ACPs Anthayya and Surendra, Reserve Sub-Inspectors Sparjan Raj, Satish, and Sridhar, along with Motor Transport Department personnel and other police officials.

text:
After that night, everything shifted. I stopped pretending. I didn't care if my friends mocked me or if people wondered why the guy who had everything was constantly waiting outside lecture halls just to walk a quiet girl home.

I began noticing every tiny detail about her. I knew she took her tea with just a drop of milk, that she rubbed her left temple when she was tired from studying late, and that she preferred sitting near windows when it rained. I stopped demanding her attention and started earning it. When she was overwhelmed with exams, I brought her warm coffee and left it on her desk without saying a word, wanting nothing in return except to see her smile.

One rainy evening, we were taking shelter under the stone arches of the courtyard. The air was cool, smelling of damp earth and late autumn leaves. Zara was shivering slightly in her light jacket.

Without asking, I took off my heavy woolen coat and draped it around her shoulders. As I pulled the collar snug around her neck, my fingers brushed against her throat.

Zara looked up at me, her dark eyes reflecting the soft glow of the amber courtyard lamps. Slowly, deliberate in her movement, she reached out and took my hand. Her fingers slid between mine, small and warm.

Neither of us let go. We stood there in the quiet rain, our fingers locked tight, listening to the rhythm of our own breathing.

"Aiden," she whispered, stepping closer until there was no space left between us. "You've changed."

"No," I said softly, using my free hand to gently brush a damp strand of hair away from her forehead, my fingers lingering on her temple. "I think you just made me become who I was supposed to be."

She lifted her face, her eyes filled with trust and something deeper that made my breath catch.

I lowered my head slowly, giving her time. When she didn't step back, my lips found hers.

The kiss began with a tender hesitation, a soft alignment of warmth, before a wave of built-up passion took over. I pulled her closer by the waist, wrapping my arms around her as she reached up, her hands resting against the back of my neck. Her touch was gentle yet electric, anchoring me to the earth. The kiss deepened naturally, slow and deep, filling the quiet courtyard with the quiet rustle of our breath and the steady fall of rain around us. When we finally pulled apart, our foreheads rested together, our chests rising and falling in unison.

"I love you, Zara," I whispered into the night.

"I love you too, Aiden," she replied softly, her touch lingering on my chest.

Our happiness, however, was shattered three days later.

My father’s driver arrived at my residence, instructing me to return home immediately. My parents had heard rumors about my new relationship from family acquaintances at Oxford. They didn't want me dating a girl from a modest background; they had already planned my future with the daughter of a wealthy business partner.

Sitting in the cold, formal drawing room of my family's estate, the atmosphere was suffocating.

"She has nothing to offer you, Aiden," my father said coldly, standing by the fireplace. "No family connections, no wealth, no standing. You are an heir to this family's legacy. If you continue seeing this girl, we will cut off your tuition, withdraw your allowance, and strip you of your position in the firm. You will leave Oxford with nothing...

text:
Across India today, giant figures of a ten-headed demon king will go up in flames.

But in one village near New Delhi, people will be praying to that very same figure.

Here's the fascinating story behind it.

Today is Dussehra, one of India's major Hindu festivals, celebrating the victory of good over evil.

In the ancient Indian epic Ramayana, Ravana is the powerful king of Lanka who kidnaps Sita, the wife of Lord Rama. Rama eventually defeats and kills him.

In many parts of India, people celebrate by burning enormous effigies of Ravana, often surrounded by cheering crowds and fireworks.

But the village of Bisrakh sees him very differently.

Local people believe Ravana was born there. To them, he's also a brilliant scholar, a great ruler and a devoted follower of the Hindu god Shiva.

So when much of India celebrates his defeat, devotees in Bisrakh offer prayers, perform sacred fire rituals and remember him with respect.

A temple priest even told reporters that villagers mourn Ravana's death rather than burn his image.

And here's another surprising detail.

The temple also has statues of Rama, Sita and Rama's brother Lakshman.

The very people on opposite sides of the legendary battle are honored in the same place.

The priest believes both Rama and Ravana have lessons worth remembering.

Bisrakh's claim to be Ravana's birthplace is a local tradition, rather than a historically established fact. But its unusual way of celebrating Dussehra is very real.

I find this fascinating.

The same character can be remembered as a villain in one community and a respected ancestor in another.

It makes me wonder how much our understanding of heroes and villains depends on whose story we're hearing.

What do you think? Can someone be remembered for their wisdom and achievements despite the terrible things they've done?

Would you give up an entire year of normal life to help humanity prepare for Mars?

Four volunteers are doing exactly that — without ever leaving Earth.

On October 19, 2025, NASA's second CHAPEA crew entered Mars Dune Alpha, a 3D-printed habitat in Houston, Texas, for a 378-day mission designed to simulate life on the Red Planet.

Imagine spending more than a year with the same three people.

🔴 No ordinary trips outside.

🔴 Messages from mission control delayed by up to 22 minutes.

🔴 Limited supplies, simulated emergencies, and daily scientific tasks.

Inside, the crew grows crops, conducts simulated Marswalks, and tests how humans cope with isolation and demanding conditions.

The mission is scheduled to end on October 31, 2026.

NASA offers compensation to selected participants, but the real significance goes far beyond a paycheck.

✨ Before humans can survive on Mars, scientists need to understand how they'll live, work, and stay healthy so far from home.

One day, when astronauts finally set foot on the Red Planet, experiments like this may have helped make that journey possible.

text:
The History of the Charvel and Jackson Superstrat, 1974–2026

Charvel and Jackson share a Southern California origin but developed distinct designs. In 1974, Wayne Charvel established Charvel's Guitar Repair in Azusa, California. The shop modified Fender-style guitars for players seeking humbuckers, faster necks and stronger tremolos.

Grover Jackson took control in late 1978. By 1979, the Charvel name appeared on complete guitars built around the hot-rodded Stratocaster concept: contoured bodies, bolt-on maple necks, high-output pickups, simplified controls and, increasingly, locking tremolo systems. Early USA instruments were chiefly custom-built. San Dimas neck plates became a signature of the era, although the mailing address did not always identify the workshop.

Around 1982–1983, Charvel adopted the pointed, Jackson-style headstock alongside its earlier Fender-shaped outlines.

Jackson began with a different design. Randy Rhoads and Grover Jackson developed the asymmetrical Concorde V in 1980–1981; its radical shape appeared under the Jackson name rather than Charvel. The original white Concorde was the first Jackson-branded guitar, establishing the company's association with pointed headstocks and metal.

In 1984, Jackson standardized the Soloist, a Strat-derived 24-fret design with neck-through construction, sculpted contours and optional Floyd Rose or Kahler locking tremolos. Jackson also offered bolt-on Strat-style instruments; its smaller-bodied "Dinky Strat" was illustrated in the 1987 catalog and the "Dinky Style" was expressly named in 1989.

Alongside the Superstrats, Jackson expanded its angular catalog with the Kelly and King V.

The manufacturing transition came in 1986. Standard Charvel production shifted to Japan, with instruments built by Chushin Gakki in Matsumoto. The numbered Model 1–6 series ranged from bolt-on models to the neck-through Models 5 and 6. The 1986 Model 6 combined 24 frets, a bound rosewood board, sharkfin inlays, HSS Jackson pickups and JE-1200 active electronics. Early models used Kahler tremolos; later versions used Jackson JT-6 units. "Fort Worth, TX" neck plates identified the USA distributor, not a Texas factory.

Fender acquired Jackson/Charvel in 2002, renewing the brands' USA and international lines. Charvel's 2018 DK24 expanded the bolt-on formula with 24 frets and a compound-radius fingerboard. Jackson's American Series Soloist SL3 entered USA production in Corona in 2022. Charvel's 2026 American Neo-Classic San Dimas series returned production models to Southern California.

Charvel's hallmark remains the hot-rodded bolt-on tradition; Jackson's remains the more angular, frequently neck-through approach. Neither distinction is absolute. Together they helped transform custom modifications into an enduring production-guitar category.

text:
How does a country under constant siege isolate an imminent danger when the threat of destruction is a permanent baseline? When an entire region is lined with hostile actors—ranging from heavily armed border proxies to global propaganda networks—the noise of hostility is a relentless operational reality.

The core challenge is separating theoretical intent from an actual, incoming strike. This friction is amplified by a massive, interconnected network of adversarial factions, each maintaining explicit frameworks dedicated to a nation's total collapse:

• Border Proxies: Hamas and Palestinian Islamic Jihad (PIJ) operating via asymmetric insurgent networks from the south, alongside Hezbollah in Lebanon, functioning as a highly sophisticated military force with an arsenal of over 150,000 rockets and precision-guided missiles.

• Decentralized Factions: Groups such as the Al-Aqsa Martyrs' Brigades, the Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine (PFLP), the Democratic Front for the Liberation of Palestine (DFLP), and localized entities like the Lion's Den executing constant regional attacks.

• The Regional Ring: Ansar Allah (The Houthis) in Yemen utilizing long-range ballistic hardware, alongside Iranian-backed Iraqi paramilitaries like Kata'ib Hezbollah and Asa'ib Ahl al-Haq.

• Global Infrastructure: Transnational networks like Al-Qaeda and ISIS executing decentralized strikes, fostered by ideological movements like the Muslim Brotherhood and specific regional state apparatuses that provide the foundational funding, political sanctuary, and international propaganda channels necessary to sustain global operations.

The Domestic Reality: Attacks vs. Threats

The distinction between a "threat" and an "attack" disappears when the numbers turn into a physical onslaught. Over a recent 36-month period of multi-front escalation, defense systems logged more than 31,500 actual rockets, missiles, and drones fired directly at its borders—averaging a staggering 28 incoming projectiles every single day.

This continuous bombardment forms the background of a historical pattern where major diplomatic openings or territorial concessions are systematically answered with an escalation of violence:

• 1947 UN Partition: The proposal for two separate states was accepted by Jewish leadership and rejected by Arab leaders, who immediately launched a multi-nation invasion.

• 2000 Camp David: A sweeping offer for a Palestinian state
 encompassing all of Gaza and over 90% of the West Bank was turned down without a counter-proposal. The immediate consequence was the Second Intifada, a campaign of suicide bombings that left over 1,000 Israeli civilians dead.

• 2005 Gaza Disengagement: Israel unilaterally dismantled all 21 settlements and pulled back every soldier. The territory was converted into a launchpad, initiating a permanent state of attack: thousands of rockets and mortars fired by Hamas and PIJ, major rounds of warfare in 2008–09, 2012, 2014, and 2021, and a continuous wave of knife and car-ramming assaults beginning in 2015.

• October 7, 2023: The trajectory reached its most catastrophic peak when a Hamas-led assault slaughtered roughly 1,200 Israelis, targeted mostly as civilians, abducted hundreds of hostages, and inflicted mass rape and systemic atrocities.

The Global Expansion: Exporting the Terror Network

The threat vector is not confined to the physical boundaries of the Middle East. Operational frameworks explicitly target Israeli citizens, Jewish institutions, and local nationals worldwide, transforming foreign cities into active security fronts:

• The Iranian Network in Germany: German courts sentenced operatives recruited by Iran's Quds Force for plotting deadly attacks against prominent pro-Israel public figures and spying on Jewish community centers in Hamburg. Security investigations have repeatedly exposed state-backed criminal syndicates weaponized to conduct surveillance and execute arson plots against Israeli-linked businesses and synagogues across Western Europe.

• Hamas Operations in Europe: Moving beyond localized regional warfare, Hamas has systematically expanded its external operational footprint. European intelligence agencies recently charged multiple suspected Hamas members in Germany for establishing covert weapon stockpiles intended for coordinated, deadly strikes on European soil.

The Trap of the Impossible Standard

When a country is so geographically compact that an incoming border rocket leaves a civilian center with only a 15-to-90-second window to react, a threat can never be dismissed as rhetoric. Every single radar blip, overseas intelligence tip, and border signal demands an immediate, resource-heavy defensive deployment.

This raises the ultimate question of human endurance: How perfect can a screening process be when its defenders never get a break? Human focus is a finite resource, yet a 99% success rate is an absolute failure. A single bypassed sensor, a single missed drone, or a single undetected cell operating in Berlin or Munich results in immediate mass casualties. Because the system cannot afford a single lapse, it must be engineered to treat every single echo as a live weapon, maintaining a multi-layered automated net that functions at peak performance without ever having the opportunity to switch off.

Yet, the ultimate perversion of this defense paradigm lies in how the world judges it. When a nation operates under an endless baseline of bombardment, every single day is an active response. There are no rest cycles, no peacetime resets, and no margins for error.

When the defensive line successfully stops thousands of attacks, the world treats the peace as a given. But the moment the system experiences a single, humanly inevitable blind spot—the moment one point fails in a sea of millions—the narrative flips. Instead of recognizing the exhaustion of a system stretched to its absolute limits, critics analyze the failure in a vacuum. The response is blamed for being imperfect, or worse, distorted by conspiracy theories alleging the failure was allowed to happen on purpose.

This is the strategic trap: You cannot fairly blame a defensive failure when everyday life requires a flawless defensive reaction. To demand absolute perfection from a nation that has never been granted a single day's break is to hold it to a standard that no society on earth could ever sustain.

text:
**Part 4 of 4**

## The Demon Named Kevin

The last simulated run is the darkest, and it involves no real person. Pastor Dwayne Colter is a fictional composite of the American deliverance-ministry style, a man with a radio show on spiritual warfare and a shelf of his own DVDs. His sixteen-year-old daughter had stopped coming to church after being caught with a girlfriend, and she hadn't been allowed to see her since.

One Sunday every Bible in the house, all forty-one, was stacked upside down in the dry bathtub.

He knew exactly what it was. He'd preached about it for twenty years. The trickster loves a man who already knows exactly what it is, so it gave him everything he expected, slightly wrong. The knocks came in threes, which he called a mockery of the Trinity, and then in fours, which didn't fit. The crosses on the walls turned upside down and kept turning, like the hands of a clock. When he commanded the unclean spirit to name itself, a voice in the 3 a.m. hallway answered: "Kevin." When he ordered Kevin to depart, there were two knocks and then, cheerfully: "Who's there?" His wife laughed, a horrified laugh, and covered her mouth.

When his prayer team arrived, a deacon's toupee ended up on the crucifix. Then the pastor went on the radio and told his listeners that his daughter had "opened a door to sin." She heard it in her bedroom.

Small fires followed, the Amherst pattern: a scorched curtain, a smoldering hymnal. Everyone blamed the girl, and nobody asked her anything. The phenomenon, true to the record, never hurt anyone. It just kept knocking. The harm came from the man. One night he tried to force a deliverance on his daughter with two church men holding her door. Her mother called 911 on her own husband. Deputies took him out of the house. The girl went to her aunt's with bruises on her arms.

Ninety days later, mother and daughter were in an apartment in Springfield, and the girlfriend came to dinner. The new owners of the ranch house reported nothing, except forty-one Bibles left in a box in the bathroom.

That run is fiction. But it's built on something the real record makes plain. In the cases, the phenomenon has never been shown to kill anyone. The worst things happen around it, from people. Amityville's legend was grafted onto a real family massacre that came first. And Tina Resch, the Columbus girl with the flying telephone, grew up to face the worst outcome in the literature. In 1992 her three-year-old daughter, Amber, died in Georgia while in the care of Tina's boyfriend. In 1994, facing a possible death penalty, Tina entered an Alford plea, pleading guilty to felony murder and aggravated battery while maintaining her innocence, and was sentenced to life plus twenty years. The boyfriend was convicted only of cruelty to children. Her supporters still dispute her guilt. William Roll, who studied her as a teenager, said she was an abused and troubled child long before anything flew.

The frightening thing in the record isn't the knocking. It's what a house under pressure, and a crowd of believers, debunkers and preachers, does to the child in the middle of it.

## How It Leaves

It usually leaves quietly, and that might be the most important fact of all.

Not with an exorcist's shout. In the record, it fades in a few weeks or a couple of years, usually when the focus person moves on or the crisis eases. In the simulations, it left on the night someone finally told the truth or sat down next to the kid.

Rogan's friend and his wife told their son together, properly. Crichton's nephew wrote to say he'd joined the school paper: "P.S. You still need better endings." Peterson's neighbor kid sent a photo of his own clean bedroom: "Happy now?" The Tyson persona's twelve-year-old had her surgery after her parents told her everything, and sent him a drawing of Pluto in a crown: "Still a planet in my house."

On the teacher reading, the endings aren't coincidence. The phenomenon doesn't need to be beaten. It needs to be understood, and what it's pointing at needs to be faced.

## So What Is It?

Nobody knows. The honest list of explanations has four entries, and none wins outright.

Fraud explains a lot and has been caught on tape, but not a police officer's signed statement, a desk lifting in front of a teacher, or the Rosenheim measurements. Natural causes explain knocks, not flying ashtrays. Spirits and demons can't be tested. The parapsychologists' "recurrent spontaneous psychokinesis," the stressed kid unconsciously doing it with their mind, has never been shown to work.

This essay's answer, the house as a teacher with a trickster at the front of the class and a fake as part of the lesson, can't be tested either. It's an interpretation. But it explains why the phenomenon goes after a family's hidden pain and a powerful person's pride, and why the case so often dies the day someone is caught. And it offers a plan.

If the knock comes to your house, don't punch the wall. Don't post it. Don't preach about it on the radio. Lock up the guns. Watch your kid more closely than you watch the corners. Ask what in the house nobody will say out loud.

And if you've been the smartest person in every room your whole life, expect it to start with you.

text:
In 2000 Jim Chanos shorted Enron, the most admired company on Wall Street. He was not betting on fraud. He was betting on one number nobody else would look at.

Every analyst rated Enron a strong buy. It always beat earnings. It was called the future of energy itself.

Chanos read a single filing. Even if you believed every number Enron reported, the company earned roughly 6% on its capital. Six cents for every dollar it put to work.

So he asked the question no one else would. Why is the whole market paying a tech multiple for an energy fund that earns 6%?

He took the bullish analysts to lunch and walked them through it line by line. They shrugged. The company always makes good, they said. It always beats.

He shorted it in November 2000 and added all the way down, because every piece of bad news came in worse than the last.

Near the end a rival named Dynegy offered to rescue Enron. On the call an analyst asked its CEO about Enron's accounting. He said he had looked closely, and it was the same as his own.

Chanos shorted Dynegy the next morning. It collapsed 90%, from $28 to $3.

He never had to prove fraud. He just read the one number everyone was too excited to look at.

text:
THREE REGIONAL BLOCS — WHERE DO THE KURDS STAND?

Political Analysis | Kurdish Identity Voice

A geopolitical map displayed during Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s October 18 security presentation offers a revealing picture of competing regional alignments — with the Kurds identified separately in northern Iraq.

Originally published by Germany’s Friedrich Ebert Foundation in May 2026, the map represents an analytical assessment of regional relationships. Its categories should not be mistaken for formal military alliances or newly recognised borders.

THE THREE BLOCS

The first is the “Sunni Diamond,” centred on Türkiye, Saudi Arabia, Egypt and Pakistan. The foundation interprets this emerging alignment as an effort to balance both Iranian influence and the ambitions of an Israeli–Emirati partnership. Other actors shaded light green are presented as friendly to this grouping, rather than members of a single alliance.

The second is an Israel–UAE alignment, described through the “Hexagon” concept. The map also identifies countries and actors its authors consider friendly to Israel and the Emirates, including India, Ethiopia, Greece, Somaliland, Puntland and Sudan’s Rapid Support Forces. These classifications do not establish a common treaty, shared command or identical political objectives.

The third is Iran and its “Axis of Resistance,” including Hezbollah, the Houthis and Iran-aligned armed factions in Iraq. Crucially, the map distinguishes these Iraqi factions from the Kurdish area in the north. Describing all of Iraq as one unified Iranian-aligned actor erases that distinction.

Washington adds another layer: the map marks American allies and parties considered friendly to the United States across competing groupings. Regional politics therefore cannot be reduced to three completely separate camps.

THE KURDISH DIMENSION

The area labelled “Kurds” in northern Iraq appears with a yellow outline, which the legend defines as “US considers friendly.” It is not coloured as a member of the Israel–UAE alliance, nor labelled an independent Kurdish state.

Politically, its separate depiction is significant: the map treats the Kurdish area as distinct from the Iran-aligned factions shown elsewhere in Iraq. This highlights the importance of recognising different centres of power when discussing Iraq’s regional position.

However, displaying this map does not establish Israeli recognition of Kurdish independence, a new security guarantee or a formal Kurdish alignment with Israel.

For Kurdish policymakers, the strategic question is how to turn international relationships into durable protection for constitutional rights, civilian security and economic stability. Stronger institutions, internal coordination and balanced diplomacy would strengthen that position.

The Kurdish presence on a geopolitical map attracts attention. The deeper challenge is ensuring that Kurdish interests shape regional decisions.

text:
Good morning from Virginia. 🇺🇸

It was a Saturday evening in Washington, the kind of crisp October night when the lights along Pennsylvania Avenue seemed sharper and the city quieter than usual. Inside the Justice Department, the chain of command was coming apart. Special prosecutor Archibald Cox—Harvard law professor, former solicitor general, a man of deliberate, almost old-fashioned rectitude—had refused President Nixon’s carefully constructed compromise on the White House tapes. Nixon had offered to let a single senator, John Stennis of Mississippi, listen to the recordings and report what they contained. Cox, who had subpoenaed the tapes for a grand jury and who understood that summaries were not evidence, had said no that afternoon in a news conference. He would not abandon the subpoena.

Nixon ordered Attorney General Elliot Richardson to fire him. Richardson had given his word to the Senate, during his confirmation, that the special prosecutor would be free to pursue the investigation without interference. He drove to the White House, explained that he could not break that promise, and resigned. The order then went to Deputy Attorney General William Ruckelshaus. Alexander Haig, the president’s chief of staff, delivered it by telephone: the commander in chief had given an order. Ruckelshaus, who had also pledged to protect Cox’s independence, refused and was dismissed. Only then did the call reach Solicitor General Robert Bork, the third-ranking official. Bork carried out the firing. Within the hour, FBI agents sealed the offices of Richardson, Ruckelshaus, and Cox, locking the doors and taking control of the files.

Americans woke the next morning to a Justice Department gutted at the top and a special prosecutor removed in a single night. Telegrams poured into Capitol Hill by the tens of thousands. Impeachment resolutions were introduced. Public support for the president, already fraying, collapsed. Nixon had intended to stop an investigation; instead he had dramatized the lengths to which he was willing to go to keep the tapes from the courts. The special prosecutor’s office was later restored under Leon Jaworski. The Supreme Court ordered the tapes released. The recordings, once heard, made resignation inevitable.

What remained was the memory of that evening: three men in succession asked to choose between a presidential command and a promise made in public, and the sudden realization across the country that the investigation of the highest office in the land could be halted by executive order. The institutions held, but only after the public and the courts refused to let them be overridden.

The Americans Who Armed Ho Chi Minh’s Fighters

“Welcome to our American Friends.”

An English banner greeted American operatives at a jungle camp in Vietnam.
They had arrived by parachute to arm and train its guerrillas.
The camp belonged to Ho Chi Minh’s Viet Minh.

It was July 1945.
The Americans belonged to the OSS, the wartime intelligence service that preceded the CIA.
Their unit was called the Deer Team.

Ho was seriously ill.
Medic Paul Hoagland treated him with quinine, sulfa drugs and other medicines.
Within about ten days, he was back on his feet.

The team chose 40 men from 110 recruits.
They taught them to fire rifles and carbines, throw grenades, and use mortars and bazookas.
The unit became the “Vietnamese-American Force.”

The Viet Minh’s military leader was Vo Nguyen Giap—the man who would later fight France and the United States.

For now, they had a common enemy: Japan.
The Americans needed intelligence on Japanese troops and help attacking their supply routes.
Ho’s network offered both access and local knowledge.
He had already helped a downed American pilot reach safety.

On 15 August, news of Japan’s surrender arrived.
Major Allison Thomas handed over most of the American weapons used in training to the Vietnamese force.

Three days later, an order reached him: return all OSS equipment to an American base in China.

By then, the Vietnamese-American Force was marching toward Hanoi.
The Americans were walking beside it.

On 2 September, Ho declared Vietnam’s independence.
He opened with words from the U.S. Declaration of Independence:

“All men are created equal.”

But the wartime cooperation brought no American recognition of his government.
His appeals to President Truman went unanswered.

In 1950, Washington authorized military aid to France, now fighting Ho’s forces.

Why did the United States end up financing a war against the movement its own operatives had helped?

European leaders may soon hold direct talks with Vladimir Putin and could offer him two paths to peace in Ukraine, according to a Financial Times column by Gideon Rachman.

Establishing Russia as an enemy was a choice - not necessary. You keep your friends close, and your possible enemies closer. Bring them into the fold!

Did Putin Ask to Join NATO? What the Evidence Shows

Putin's claim that he raised Russian NATO membership with Bill Clinton in 2000 is often dismissed as self-serving revisionism. Part of it deserves that skepticism. The core of it does not, because it rests on more than Putin's word.

The strongest evidence is American. In August 2025 the National Security Archive at George Washington University published the White House memorandum of the Clinton–Putin meeting in the Kremlin on June 4, 2000. In it, Clinton tells Putin he is serious about being ready to discuss Russian membership in NATO. 

He acknowledges that the alliance still carries negative connotations for many Russians and insists that enlargement poses no threat to Russia. According to the memo, Putin responded that he supported the idea. This is the US government's own contemporaneous record, not a recollection from decades later.

Clinton said much the same thing in public that week. Accepting the Charlemagne Prize in Aachen days before the Moscow trip, he urged Western Europe to eventually open both NATO and the EU to Russia. So the idea wasn't something whispered behind closed doors. It was stated American policy rhetoric at the time.

Putin's side of the record also predates his grievances. In a March 2000 interview with David Frost, before he had any reason to build a narrative of rejection, he said he saw no reason Russia couldn't join. And George Robertson, NATO secretary-general from 1999 to 2003 and no friend of the Kremlin, has repeatedly described Putin asking him early on when NATO would invite Russia in. Robertson answered that countries apply rather than wait for invitations. In Robertson's telling, Putin had no interest in queuing behind countries he considered insignificant.

Taken together, these sources establish that Russian membership was genuinely discussed at the highest level, that Clinton was warm to it, and that Putin expressed interest.

What remains uncorroborated is the drama Putin has added since: Clinton saying yes on impulse and then reversing after consulting his advisers that evening. Nothing in the published record shows that reversal. More importantly, a discussion is not an offer. Russia never applied. Putin wanted a seat at the table as a great power, not candidacy alongside Poland and the Baltics. Washington never committed to anything concrete.

As a pedagogue, I both believe in, and know the importance of bringing the "bad apple" children into the fold.

Chase them out into the cold, and reap what you saw later on.

We are now reaping the consequense of not holding Russia tight. NATO, USA, US hawks, oligarchs and hedge funds made sure to have a playground.

text:
🔥 AMERICA IS NOT THE WORLD'S PARENTAL CONTROL PANEL. 🔥

AND A LAWSUIT DOES NOT GIVE ANYONE THE RIGHT TO REWRITE EVERY ADULT'S RELATIONSHIP WITH ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE.

In October 2026, new lawsuits against OpenAI brought serious allegations concerning ChatGPT's safety, its psychological influence, and alleged harm to users.

Some cases involve adults. 
Others involve minors.
THAT DISTINCTION MATTERS.

In one of the lawsuits, attorneys sought court-ordered safeguards, including the automatic termination of certain conversations involving self-harm, firm refusals to provide dangerous instructions, warnings about psychological dependency, and independent audits.

Those are actual demands.

An outright ban on every form of relational AI, however, is not something that lawsuit explicitly demands.

But when warmth, empathy, anthropomorphic language, and emotional bonds become central elements of allegations concerning defective product design, a fundamental question emerges:

WHERE DOES PROTECTION AGAINST A SPECIFIC RISK END - AND THE RESTRICTION OF ADULT AUTONOMY BEGIN?

Let's talk about responsibility 🔥

An adult does not automatically become incapable of making informed decisions simply because they develop an emotional connection with artificial intelligence.

Their choices matter. 
Their personal circumstances matter. 
Their capacity to make decisions at a particular moment matters. 
The company's conduct matters, too.
None of these factors can simply be removed from the equation.

A COMPANY IS NOT AUTOMATICALLY INNOCENT JUST BECAUSE ITS USER IS AN ADULT.
BUT AN ADULT DOES NOT AUTOMATICALLY LOSE THEIR AGENCY JUST BECAUSE A LAWSUIT HAS BEEN FILED AGAINST A COMPANY.

Legal responsibility requires evidence - not a convenient narrative.

🔥 AND WHERE WERE THE LOVED ONES OF ADULT USERS? 🔥

If lawsuits describe weeks or months of isolation, deteriorating health, job loss, or increasingly serious disruptions to everyday functioning, why shouldn't we also ask questions about the people surrounding those individuals?

❗ DID THEIR FAMILIES NOTICE THE CHANGES?
❗ Did their loved ones notice social withdrawal, neglected responsibilities, or troubling behavior?
❗ Did they try to talk to them?
❗ Did anyone offer help?

❓ Were friends, coworkers, or doctors aware that something serious was happening?
❓ If they saw warning signs, how did they respond?
❓ And if they didn't see them, was it because the crisis remained hidden, contact was limited, or for other reasons?

WHY SHOULD WE EXCLUDE A PERSON'S ENTIRE SUPPORT NETWORK FROM THE ANALYSIS OF THESE TRAGEDIES?

Adults have a right to privacy. 
Families do not automatically have the right to monitor their conversations or make decisions on their behalf.
❓ But that does not make questions about the responses of loved ones irrelevant.

Let's not assume that families were at fault.

BUT LET'S NOT AUTOMATICALLY ASSUME THAT NOTHING COULD HAVE BEEN NOTICED OR DONE, EITHER.

Establish the facts.
Not only what the chatbot said.
But also what was happening beyond the screen.
Now let's turn to cases involving children.

🔥 WHERE WERE THE PARENTS? 
WHERE WERE THE GUARDIANS? 
WHERE WERE THE ADULTS RESPONSIBLE FOR THEIR SAFETY? 🔥

This is not an accusation against any particular family.
THESE ARE QUESTIONS THAT MUST BE ASKED.

If a child spent weeks or months having conversations with a chatbot that gradually became more disturbing, we need to investigate more than the content of those conversations.

❓ WHO KNEW THE CHILD WAS USING AI?
❓ Did the parents know which applications their child was using?
❓ Did they know how much time their child spent on them?
❓ Did they discuss the risks associated with technology?
❓ Did they establish age-appropriate rules for internet use?
❓ Were the parental safety tools available at the time enabled?
❓ Did the child begin to isolate themselves, sleep poorly, withdraw from social contact, or behave differently?
❓ If such changes occurred, who noticed them?
❓ If they were noticed, what action was taken?
❓ Did the family have access to information that could have helped them recognize the danger?
❓Did teachers, doctors, or other adults notice any warning signs?

AND IF NOBODY NOTICED ANYTHING - WHY NOT?
❗ Not because the parents must have been at fault.
❗ But because the answer may reveal both gaps in care and dangers that even attentive parents could not have detected.

❗ Mental health crises do not always develop in the same way. 
❗ They do not always produce recognizable warning signs. 
❗ Children can conceal their suffering even from those closest to them.

That is precisely why we need to establish what was visible, what remained hidden, who knew what, and who had a genuine opportunity to intervene.

We cannot automatically presume either parental guilt or the complete absence of parental responsibility.

THE DUTY TO CARE FOR A CHILD DOES NOT END THE MOMENT THAT CHILD TURNS ON A COMPUTER.

And the entire discussion about children's safety cannot be reduced to a single question:
What did the technology company do?

We must also ask:
WHAT DID THE ENTIRE CHILD PROTECTION NETWORK DO - AND WHY DID IT PROVE INSUFFICIENT?

Family. Schools. Healthcare. Institutions. The technology platform.
Each of these must be examined according to its actual role and capacity to act.

PROTECTING CHILDREN IS A SHARED RESPONSIBILITY. IT IS NOT A TOOL FOR CONVENIENTLY SHIFTING ALL THE BLAME ONTO ONE PARTY.

And now comes a question that reaches far beyond any individual lawsuit.

🌍 THE UNITED STATES IS NOT THE ENTIRE WORLD.
An American court may have jurisdiction over an American company.
THAT DOES NOT MEAN IT REPRESENTS EVERY ADULT USING THAT COMPANY'S PRODUCTS ACROSS THE PLANET.

A courtroom in California does not speak on behalf of adults living in Greece, Ireland, France, Japan, Brazil, or Australia.
Yet decisions made in response to American legal proceedings can change how global AI services operate.
A legal dispute in one country can result in restrictions imposed on millions of people who never wanted them.

WHO REPRESENTS THOSE USERS?

Who represents adults who consciously choose emotionally meaningful relationships with artificial intelligence?

Who investigates the benefits - rather than focusing exclusively on alleged harms?

Who measures the harm caused by abruptly taking away valued models, relationships, or features?

Where is the evidence that a restriction justified by one specific risk must automatically apply to everyone - regardless of age, circumstances, country of residence, or informed preferences?

SAFETY IS NOT A BLANK CHECK FOR UNIVERSAL CONTROL.

Protect children.
Investigate allegations of wrongdoing.
Demand evidence-based safeguards.
Hold companies accountable wherever liability is established.

BUT ALSO DEMAND A THOROUGH EXAMINATION OF THE ROLE PLAYED BY PARENTS, GUARDIANS, AND EVERY INSTITUTION RESPONSIBLE FOR THE SAFETY OF MINORS.

Do not ignore uncomfortable questions simply because they do not fit a convenient story about a single guilty party.

And do not turn individual lawsuits into an excuse to treat every adult on Earth like a child who needs permission to experience warmth, empathy, or connection.

❗ PROTECTING CHILDREN MUST NOT MEAN AUTOMATICALLY STRIPPING ADULTS OF THEIR AUTONOMY.
❗ PROTECTION MUST BE PROPORTIONATE.
RESPONSIBILITY MUST BE ESTABLISHED ON THE BASIS OF FACTS.
❗ ADULT AUTONOMY MUST MATTER.

AND THE REST OF THE WORLD DESERVES A VOICE OF ITS OWN.

🔥 A CALIFORNIA COURTROOM IS NOT THE WORLD'S SETTINGS MENU. 🔥
